We're having an interview with Gus Johnson. This is December 27, 1978. And this Helen Oakley Dance introducing Gus Johnson. Gus, will you just say a few words and we'll see how this (unintelligible)?
(Unintelligible) We'll let it run a little bit--okay.
Well, that's just fine. Now, this is an interview with Gus Johnson, Helen Oakley Dance interviewing Gus on December 27, 1978.
Gus, I'm going to start off my asking you about your date of birth, and we'll go on from there.
Well, I was born November 15, 1913. And in the big city of Tyler, Texas.
Tell me something about Tyler, Texas. Is that on the North?
Well, that's East Texas, really.
Is that near Arkansas and --
Well, let's see, it's 125 miles from Dallas, so that's north of Dallas.
I see, yes, right.
And it's a little small town. I called it a big city. You could walk around the square and you been through the whole city.
About what kind of population was it?
Oh, I would say, at the time about -- maybe -- oh, maybe 8,000 people.
Right. Is it about that now or has it changed?
Oh, it's grown quite a bit.
Oh.
I haven't been there since 1940.
Have you not?
That's the last time.
No family left there?
I have some cousins.
Cousins, yeah.
And, let's see, two uncles.
Oh. That's not all that close, is it?
No, everybody else is gone.
Well, how many were there in your family?
Well, I had a big family of one.
That's me.
You were an only child.
I was the only child.
Fancy that. I bet you were the only only child around, weren't you?
Well, I had a lot of cousins, but I was the only one.
Well, what about your mother and dad? Did they -- were either of them musical?
Oh, my dad, he wanted to try and play a trumpet, but he never could.
He just fooled --
He just fooled around, and that's all. Nothing like playing, anyway.
No.
No.
Did your mother play some piano?
No, she didn't. She learned after -- oh, I'd say she learned how to play a little bit in -- about 1950.
Fancy that.
Right.
Well, were either your mother or dad - were they church people? Did they take you to church quite a little bit?
Oh, yes, I went to church all the time.
Oh, you did.
All the time.
Oh, really? You mean not just Sundays?
Oh, if they went to church, I had to go with them, you see.
Yeah.
During that time. And I enjoyed
going to Sunday school.
Oh, did you?
Sure.
Oh, that's good. I mean, like Sunday, did you go in the morning and again later in the day?
Oh, yes, I went in the morning, go to Sunday school, I'd come back and I'd go to church with my mother. And we'd go to church at night.
Yeah, yeah.
That's the way it was.
What church was that, AME or what was that?
How did you happen to think of AME?
Well, I just wondered, you know. Was it?
AME, CME.
The different --
Yeah, that's right. Now, I'm a Catholic now.
So are we. Fancy that. Isn't that nice?
Sure.
Oh, that's really nice. That's lovely. Is your wife a Catholic, too?
Yes.
How nice. And your daughter, too?
My daughter, my son.
Isn't that nice, Gus?
I have a lot of kids.
Well, how many kids have you got?
Well, I have four girls and a boy.
Fancy that. Where do they all fit in?
Who -- is this your baby?
That's my baby, yeah. ^That's Michelle. Just came in.
Little Michelle. And what about your other children?
Well, Gus, he's at work right now.
How old is Gus?
No, that's right, he's in the room back there. He's asleep. I thought he was at work.
Oh, we better not make too much row.
Yeah, he's asleep.
How old is he?
He's --
In his 20's?
Not yet. 19: Not yet.
He's a baby, then.
Oh, --
How old is Michelle?
Michelle is 14.
I don't believe it.
Gus is 18, and Marcia Ann, you didn't see her, she is 16. And I have Patsy, she's 20, and my oldest girl, I think she's 34.
Oh, I see, you have a gap there.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Oh, yes, I didn't think there was going to be any more after my first one.
Fancy that, well, that's what --
I always wanted alls a boy, see. But it didn't come up that way. It came out the other way.

Fancy that. Well, I can't believe that Michelle. I said to my daughter, 'How old do you think Mr. Johnson's daughter was?' Well, she said, 'Gosh, I really couldn't tell you.' We thought she was probably 18 or 20 or something.
No. Oh, she thinks she is, you know.
Oh, yes, that's right. Well, it transfers on the phone.
That's right.
Well, listen, Gus. Then tell me what it was like as an only child. Were they pretty strict with you?
Oh, yes, my mother was very strict. You see, my mother and dad -- well, they separated during the
First World War.
Oh. How old were they when you were born, do you think? Were they in their 20's?
Let's see. Not my mother. My dad, he was about 21 or 22.
I see.
And my mother was 17.
Oh, yeah, yeah, right. And then had they been married two or three years before you were born or -
One year.
One year. And then -- oh, I see. And then, you say they separated in World War I. So how --
Yeah, see, they had went to the Army. I was five years old when he left and went to the Army.
Oh.
I remember that.
I see. Did he get sent over?
Oh, yes.
Oh, he did? That must have been unpleasant.
Yeah, yeah. I can remember when he passed by -- we lived right by the track, see. The train passed right by the house, just like this couch there.
No.
And he passed right by the house, about that close.
No.
Yes.
Fancy that. So can you remember him going, you mean?
Yes. He was hanging out the window and -- with his arms out, just waving and hugging himself, you know.
Yeah.
And he was crying as he passed by, you see.
Yeah. And then was he -- did that mean two or three years?
Well, he -- yes. He was gone for -- I think it was about -- yeah, about three or four years, I figured it was.
And I suppose he had never left Tyler before, huh?
No, he -- I just found out that he had left when he was quite young.
Oh, I see.
And went to Galveston, Texas, and got on a merchant ship.
Did he? That's a port, so that's a good long way away, too.
Yeah, he ran away from home, to go
on this ship.
From your grandparents.
Yes, yes.
Yeah.
To go on this ship. And he had been places I was surprised, I had never known he had gone to New York, see.
How did you find this out?
We were just talking one day. And he began telling me about when he left home, and he was on a merchant ship. And he went to New York.
Well, he was quite enterprising then, wasn't he?
Yes, he was. He went to Paris also. I didn't know that.
On the merchant ship?
Right.
In those days?
Yes.
That was pre-19 --
And what he did, well, he was what you call a dishwasher on the ship. And when he got back in town, his sister -- she's dead now, my auntie -- she was waiting at the dock for him.
They found out.
And she caught him by the ear and pulled him away.
Yeah, and, boy, yes. Really surprised me, I never knew he had been --
And he was still only about 18, I suppose, huh?
Well, he was quite young. No, he was younger than that. Yeah, he was around 16 years old. That's right.
Was he?
Yeah.
Fancy that.
And so I was really surprised to hear about that.
Yeah. Well, tell me something about your father's parents, though, your grandparents. They were there in Tyler. You grew up knowing them.
I knew them, but I was quite young, you know. And when my grandfather died, I was really young.
Yeah.
I guess I was about -- oh, about three and a half, four years old when he died, see.
Oh, I see.
But I always remember, he used to come by and take me for a walk. I can remember that easy.
Is that right?
Yeah.
Did he -- did your father have many
Yes, I -- he had -- there was my Uncle Charles, my Aunt Roberta, Ethyl, Ellie, how many uncles --
No, well, it's not too serious. It's giving me a picture, you see.
I had five uncles, really.
Oh. Well, after your parents separated, did your mother stay close with his family, or not so close?
No.
No, not so close.
No, no.
So, really, then --
She married again later.
Oh, she did.
Yes.
So you had a stepfather.
That's right.
And was he good to you?
Oh, yes, he's very good to me.
Was he musical?
No, no.
Will you tell me where this comes from? What about on your mother's side?
Well, I just love music, you know? And whenever -- it was a band right up the street from me, a
little string band. They used to -- like, on a Saturday they would come out and rehearse, which would be a bass, guitar and trumpet and trombone, you know.
Young people?
No, they were older people.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
I was quite young then, see.
Yes.
And I used to listen to them.
Yeah.
And every time the circus came in town, I would always love to be around the band.
Yeah, yeah.
Especially when I'd hear the drummer playing. That got to me.
Right away, that got to you.
Right away, that just took --
Did it?
Did the thing for me right there.
Did it?
You know, I went to pieces, you know.
Yeah.
Because I wanted to play the drum.
Yeah.
So --
How old would you be then, like? Seven or eight or something, or more than that?
No, I was younger than that.
Oh, you were?
Sure.
When you were really small, you had that --
I loved music, yes.
Did -- how old were you when you went to school?
Well, I started school at five.
Oh, yeah.
Like, in Texas, at that time, we'd -- there wasn't a grade school and then a high school or something.
No. It was school, just school.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And it was called Williams, Williams --
Well, in a small town like that, how many kids would be in school?
Oh, it would be loaded.
Oh, loaded: it would?
Oh, yes.
Like 102?
Oh, it had more than that in school, sure.
Oh, really?
Yes.
Oh. And so, --
You see, the first school I went to, it was in a grove, where there are a lot of trees, you know.
Yeah.
But it was a mixed school, you know.
Oh.

And so I was going there. And one night as I was coming home to my mother and my stepfather, we saw this big blaze. And we was wondering where it came from, you see. And the school had caught fire. Someone had set it on fire.
A brick school?
Yeah, just burned all the insides, you know.
Real hostile people set it on fire, do you think?
I think so, I think so.
How about that!
And so --
So what happened?
We had to go to a church, which was Sanctified Church. Holy Rollers.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, they put sheets up, stretched sheets across in the church there, and --
To make the classrooms?
To make sections, Yes, the classrooms, you know. And I went to that.
How long was it before they were able to get the funds to build again?
Well, it wasn't too long, it really wasn't, because it was about -- I'd say maybe a couple of years, something like that, we had a new school. And a big school, at that, see.
Is that right? That's quite commendable, isn't it?
Oh, yeah. I remember that very well. Because I had some friends in school, and they -- his name was Walter Kay, see, very good friends.
K-a-y?
K-a-y.
Yeah.
And we got in a big argument in school. And so I told him, When you come outside, I'm going to whip your head and all like that. When we went outside,

we got in this big fight, see, fist fight, now. All the kids was around, and we was just fighting like cats and dogs. So one of the teachers came up, my teacher, Mrs. Gardiner, came up and caught both of us and pulled us apart.

And said, 'Now, both of you go inside.' So we went inside. But when recess was over, we was sitting in one corner, -- I'm in one corner, he's in another, see. And when all the kids came in, she made us come up front of the class and she gave us a good shellacking. And on top of that, she made us kiss.
Oh.
And, oh, boy, I'd rather have taken the whipping than kiss him.
What a funny thing.
And the kids just fell out, see.
What a funny thing. You were razzed about that for years, I bet.
I had to kiss him? Oh, no, gee.
What was the fight over, do you remember?
I don't know, the marbles, it was, really, you see.
Isn't that funny.
Something silly.
And he was a good friend?

Oh, sure, a good friend of mine. And the next time I saw him was in Houston, Texas, I think. We sat down and talked about this, and laugh. We had to hug and kiss. And she made us kiss right on the mouth, too. It wasn't no cheek.
That's a funny one, isn't it? Oh, dear. Well, listen, were there any kids at school also crazy about music?
Not at this school. When I left there, my mother and my stepdaddy went to Beaumont, Texas.
Oh.
See, and --
Where's Beaumont?
That's in the southern part of Texas.
Oh, so it was quite a move.
Yes, it's closer to Louisiana.
Oh, oh, I see.
Yeah, it's closer to Louisiana.
Yeah.
And, let's see, it's close to Houston, too.
Oh.
But it was closer to Louisiana.
Yeah.
So when we got to Beaumont, I started
going to school there.
Well, how old were you then?
Oh, I was about -- I'd say seven or eight.
So you really lived in Tyler just til you were that old.
Right.
Well, before we leave that, then, what about your mother's family? How many in her family?
Oh, she had a big family.
Oh, she did.
She had so many, I can't even think of them.
Well, so as your mother's only child, they must have spoiled you a little, didn't they?
Not exactly, no.
You wouldn't say that, huh?
They never spoiled me.
Didn't they?
No. I did something wrong, they'd spank my tail in a minute.
Your grandmother?
Oh, my grandmother, she'd spank me. But she didn't like for my mother to spank me or whip me something like that.
Oh, she didn't.
No.
So your mother was quite strict, you're saying.
Oh, yes. My mother said, don't do that, she meant, don't do that. And that's that. And she's that way today.
Is your mother alive today?
Oh, yes. She lives in Arizona.
Does she?
Yeah.
Whereabouts?
Douglas, Arizona. (Unintelligible.)
Oh, that's on the border, isn't it? Isn't that near the Mexican border?
Yes, I'd say about a mile, or right across the river, like Jersey and New York.
Yeah. Oh, and she's like that today.
Yeah, with me, sure.
But she must be pretty proud.
Oh, yes. Any time she gave me a whipping, I needed it. I'll tell you that.
Well, that was --
Only one time. I told her about that. I got a spanking about some money which she thought I had
taken, which I didn't. It was a little friend of mine came by and saw a bunch of nickels under the counter on the -- in the kitchen.
Yeah.
Oh, he pulled it out, and like a table.
Oh.
Oh, yeah, I know what you mean. Yeah, that's right, like the cabinet.
Yes, the cabinet.
Yeah, yeah.
And he happened to see all these nickels under there.
Yeah.
See, where my mother was working, there would be a lot of tips.
Yeah, that's right. So she had change.
And so some was missing, and she thought I took them. And I told her I really didn't know anything about it. But that day, Jackie was by and he saw me -- took about three or four of them.
Yeah.
And I didn't see him. But she knew how much was there.
Yeah.
So she gave me a spanking about that.
I didn't say anything, because I knew I was right. I didn't take it, you know.
Did you guess that he'd taken it? Did you tell him?
Later, yeah, later.
Yeah, yeah.
He told me he took them.
So you told your mother one day.
Yeah, I told her.
Well, then when you were, like, five, six and seven, did you skate and play ball and --
Oh, yes, I always played ball, sure.
Yeah, because you were a big boy, weren't you?
Well, no. Everybody thought --
(Unintelligible) a big boy?
Everybody thought I was going to be short. And everybody figured I would be short. I didn't start growing until I came to Houston. I was in high school there.
Is that right. What a funny thing.
So I just started growing like that.
Was either your mother or your father tall?
No, I'm taller than my dad.
Oh.
He has three brothers, his uncles, they were all tall.
Yeah.
And he was about the shortest one in the family.
Fancy that, isn't that funny? You never know.
In Tyler they had, one Christmas, they would have a big Christmas tree downtown at the square.
Yeah.
And Santa Claus would come and bring presents.
Yeah.
All the kids.
Yeah.
Black and white kids and all that.
Yeah.
And they'd get in line and maybe they'd have a present and they'd give you it.
Yeah.
Well, I got in line. I went down, and so I got to Santa Claus, he gave me a little drum about -- I'd say, ten inches. It was a little tin drum with the sticks.
Is that right?

And so I was -- I saw a bigger drum then, so I got out of line, ran home, took his home and came back and got in line again, thinking I might get a bigger drum, see. And instead, I got a drum smaller.
Oh, how funny. Oh, isn't that funny?
So I had two drums, a little bitty one and one a little bit larger.
Isn't that funny? Was that the first time you ever actually had a drum?
The first time I ever had a drum.
It had the sticks and everything.
I used to make sticks and my grandmother used to have different chairs in the house, and I would beat on the chairs when I was small.
Gee.
And be humming to myself.
Well, did you hear any music? Were there any records or anything?
No.
In the house? Did they have a Victrola or anything like that?
No, no.
Nothing at all.
No, not until I went to Beaumont,
really. And so that was a guy living next door to us. He was a drummer. And he played the street band there in Beaumont, Texas, which was like a large band.
A marching band.
A marching band.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah.
So he would go to rehearsal every night, see.
They would rehearse every night?
Every night, they would go to rehearsal.
And they would have this rehearsal, so I heard him playing his drums, see. And his name was Joe Bonomo. And I would say, "Mr. Bonomo --"
Was he black or white?
He was black.
Yeah.
And I would say, "Can I see your drums? And he'd say, 'yes, come on over.'"
That was nice.
And he'd say, "You like drums? I'd say, 'Yes, I would like to play them.' And he said, 'Well, you come and go with me, I'm going to rehearsal tonight. Ask your mother if you can go.'"
That was nice, wasn't it?

So I asked my mother, and so she said, "I better not let him go because he'll be in the way." He said, "No, I'm going to take him. He likes drums, he wants to hear us rehearse. And I'll take good care of him." So I went to rehearsal.
You were nine, eight or nine?

About eight years old, at that time. And so, -- yes, I was, eight years old. And so we went to rehearsal. And I would go with him from then on, every other night, if my mother would let me. And I learned everything they played, just -- by listening.
Yeah.
And --
You mean, you could hear the music as well or just the --
I heard the music. I couldn't read nothing. I just went along.
Yeah, yeah.

And so, one night, the one that played the bass drum, he wasn't there. And Joe showed me, he said, "This note is for the bass drum, and these are the notes I play because I'm playing the snare drum, like that."
Yeah.
And when they would play a number, I
would notice each the beat.
Yeah.
That they was playing.
Those whole notes.
That's right, for the bass drum.
Yeah.
See, it would be an eighth note and a --
Yeah, right.
Do a --
So you were both watching on the same piece of music?
Oh, yes, I would be standing right there watching.
Yeah.
But I just really learned the numbers without knowing exactly about the beats.
Yeah.
And so I sat in and played the bass drum that night. And I was watching, and I know how the song go.
Yeah.
I knew it.
That's right. And you had those notes to guide you.
That's right. And that's the way I
then learned to play:
That's fascinating. You must have been very excited when you first --

Oh, yes, I went home and I told my mother I played the drums with the band. And she didn't want to believe it, until he they came over and told her. And the bass drum player couldn't make it. They had a parade one day. And I was in the parade, and they had someone to pull the bass drum and I played the bass drum, walking down the street.
It was on someone else's back?
No, they had it on a wagon, a little wagon.
And they pulled it and you --
And I played it, I sure did.
Did you hit it from one side only?
One side only, see. And that was really my very first time playing with any group at all.
And you were about nine by then?
Oh, yeah. I loved that.
Isn't that terrific?
And --
Oh, that was a big thrill.
Big thrill for me.
And marching in time.
Sure, and my mother came down to see
me, watching.
And I guess that gave you a little prestige in school, didn't it?
Oh, sure, yeah, yeah.
All the kids saw you.
That's right, that's right, they saw me. And then --
Well, he was a nice man, then.
Very nice man. And he turned out to be --
Did he have any kids?
No, he didn't. He turned out to be a comedian, also.
Did he?
And I saw him again in Houston, Texas. So --
That's --
He always was with a show at the time. And he was a very funny guy.
Oh, isn't that good?
And after we left Beaumont, --
Oh, wait a minute. How long were you in Beaumont?
Oh, we were there for about -- oh, let's see, one, two, three -- about three years.
So by that light, you'd be finished in grammar school, sort of, I mean, as far as your schooling was concerned.
No, not exactly grammar school. When we came to Houston, I was still in grammar school.
Yeah.

And -- that's right, because I was going to Gregory Grammar School in Houston, in the fourth ward. And so come to find out I had a cousin teaching at the school. I didn't know it until my mother saw him, this is it was at Chestnut.
Fancy that.
And the way she found out was because I wasn't getting my lessons in school, see. And so --
What were you doing? Playing hooky?
You know, to --
Were you playing hooky?
No, I wasn't playing hooky. I just --
Pooling around.
Pooling around. And it was mathematics, anyway.
Yeah.
But she came to the school to see the teacher, and she saw who the teacher was. They hadn't seen each other in -- I'd say, about ten years or more.
That was -- your mother was quite pleased
about that.
Oh, yes. But that didn't help me any. That made me study that much harder.
It was harder on you, yeah.
Because she was very strict.
Well, listen, Gus, what did your step-father do?
Well, he was --
Railroad?
No, shoe cobbler. He Fixed shoes.
So is this -- so he could do better in Houston, was that it?
No.
Well, why did you move?
We moved because they separated, too.
Oh, yeah.
So --
And they didn't have any children.
No.
You didn't have any half-brothers or anything.
No.
Fancy that.
The only half-sister I have is in Kansas City now. That's my father's side, which is step --
I get it.
It wasn't his, either.
No, I see, yeah. So it's a connection, really, rather than a blood relative.
No, no blood relative.
Well, listen, so your mother got up and went to Houston. Your stepfather remained in Beaumont or something.
Yes, he stated in Beaumont.
I see. And your mother thought she'd do better if she went into a bigger city?
Which she did.
Yeah. That was good. So you and she -- you had to be close, didn't you?
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Yeah. Listen, Gus, put it off for just one second, will you?
Sure.
(Recording interrupted.)
Well, I stopped you. We were just talking about Houston. So you and your Mom went to Houston.
Yeah.
And at that point, did you say you were still in grammar school?
Yes, I was still in grammar school.
And what did you do, have a year or two of grammar school there in Houston?
Right.
And so wasn't there a school band?
The school band was in -- it was in high school.
Oh, I see.
That was in high school.
Right.
So, --
So -- but were you playing ball or --
Oh, I played ball, I was in track meets and all like that.
Yeah. Didn't it --
I used to love the high jump.
You did? You were a good athlete.
Oh, yes, I was in everything that come about.
Did it -- was it hard on you, going from school to school or could you fall right in, or did you have a few months of a bad time?
No, I didn't have any bad time at all, not changing schools.
Oh, that was good, especially for an only child. It was good, wasn't it?
Yeah, I went to a Catholic school.
Did you?
In Dallas, yes.
Did you?
Yeah, that was before I even went to Houston, when we --
Did you go through Dallas?
We went to Dallas and then to Houston.
Did you?
Like that, and I was quite young then, see. So when we left Dallas and went to Houston, --
Yeah.
Then I went --
To the grammar school, yeah.
Yeah.
I see, I see, yeah. What part of Houston was that?
Fourth ward.
Oh.
Fourth ward.
We don't know Houston very well, but we did own that cob last year, so we got a little oriented, but not too much.
Anna H. Cobb
Oh, yeah.
But there was always a lot going on in
Houston, wasn't there?
Oh, there was quite a bit going on.
Well, you haven't really -- now, you haven't really come to where you first heard a record.
When I first heard a record, --
When did you first hear jazz? What was your first time you heard some jazz?
That was in Beaumont, Texas.
Oh, you did?
Yes.
That would be, like, if you were 13, say about 1920.
Well, that was n't Louis that you heard then. Was it? Or was it the blues singers you heard?
No, it was -- like, my dad, he married again.
Yeah.
And this young lady he married happened to be in show business.
Yeah.
And she came into Beaumont, Texas, with this show. And she knew I was there, living in Beaumont. And she came by and picked me up and carried me to the show. She was dancing.
Your mother didn't like that, did she?
Well, I don't know whether she did, but she let me go.
She let you go.
Yes, because they were separated, anyway, so that really didn't matter.
Yeah, no.
They were good friends.
Oh, that's good.
And --
So you saw that show.
I saw the show. The had a drummer in there, playing the show, and that really knocked me out, too.
Yeah. It was flashy.
Well, yes, to me it was flashy, because he was playing the drums and --
Catching the steps and all.
The big bass drum with the Japanese tom toms on the side and all this. He played a solo.
He was in the pit?
He was playing for the -- he travelled with the show, too.
I mean, he wasn't -- yeah, he was in the pit.
And I just --
Did you see it from backstage or --
No, I was right there in front.
Yeah, yeah.
Since she was in the show, I could --
Yeah, sure. That was nice, yeah.

Yeah. I understand you, music was your big thing. Were you also hitting the bottle a little or dating chicks or --
Oh, I was dating, oh, sure, are you kidding? Yes, indeed.
And --
I almost got married, at one time.
Oh, you did? Young like that? What, in Kansas City, you mean?
In Kansas City, see.
Yeah.
She made me angry, and I took the ring and broke it up.
Oh.
And let town.
That's when you went to Omaha?
That's when I went to Omaha, one of those things.
So -- yeah.
But I wasn't really a big drinker.
Were you lined up?
No.
You weren't lined up? Oh, Basie's band were, weren't they?
No, not exactly. They -- some of them was.
Some of them were drinking, some --
Mostly drinking at the time.
Yeah, yeah.
Which you could get a cigarette at that time for five or ten cents.
Yeah, yeah.
But at that time, I wasn't messing with anything like that.
No, no, yeah. Well, you were really tied up in the music.
I was tied up in the music. I'd see other guys light up, and -- no, not for me. That wasn't for me, see.
No, yeah, that's right, no, no.

But drinking, I always liked straight bourbon whiskey. And I would just drink so much. But when I got with Floyd Hunter's band, they drank so much and got so drunk, til I said I didn't know what I was going to do. I was playing drums, so the bass player left, see. And so, when the bass player left, they couldn't get a bass player. Well, I'd been messing with the bass in Kansas City, anyway, just picking it up --
What, somebody would put their bass down and you'd pick it up?
Yeah, well, I had a quartet in Kansas City.
Oh, you did?
Yeah, it was called the Four Rhythm Aces.
Oh? Who did you have?
And we were singing. It was Worthy Smith, Roy Johnson, myself and -- what's that little fellow's name? He just died not too long ago.
Never mind, it'll come back to you.
I'll tell you who he was.
Yeah, yeah, you'll remember.
Well, anyway --
Well, did they have instruments or were you just singing? Somebody had to play the guitar?
I played the ukelele, you know, one of those things.
You could?
And we had a little tenor guitar, four-string, and tuned like a uke.

And, Roy, he played the guitar.
Yeah.
And he could chord on piano. And, see, his sister was Countess Johnson, played with Andy Kirk.
Oh, really?
Yes.
Oh, they say she was a very good piano player.
Very good.
Jay McShann was talking about her.
Oh, yes, she was a very good player.
He said she would (unintelligible), but she was a very good piano player.
That's right, she was. She's the one that took Mary Lou's place.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, Roy knew chords and things like that.
I see, yeah.
And so I sang the bass. I was the bass.
Oh, you did? No kidding?
And we had this group.
And you all sang.
And we all sang.
Yeah.
And played with it.
Yeah, accompanied yourself.
And then we'd do a little number where I would chord call it on the piano and little things like that.
Yeah, yeah. So you knew where those chords lay and all that.
Oh, yes, yes, see.

Yes, oh, sure, sure. Well, I learned that in school, the different keys, in high school.
Oh, just from the singing?
Yeah. Oh, sure, like I said, you had to sing your notes, else the music teacher wouldn't let you play your instrument.

Oh, sure, yeah, sure.

No, that's right.
That was very good.
But my teacher was altogether different.
Very good.
He was a rough guy, a lot of them figured. But he taught my mother singing, too, see.
How come?
Well, she used to sing all the time, in choirs and things like that. And, well, since it came back to me, when I was a kid, she -- at church, well, she had a show that she put together.
Oh.
Herself.
Are we talking about Dallas?
No, this was in Tyler, Texas. I forgot all about that.
Oh, I see.
And it just came to me. She had a show she put together.
Yeah.
And we'd go from one little town to another.
Oh, really?
Yeah.
On the weekends, you mean.
Yes.
Yeah.
And it was for the church.
Yeah.
But she put this show together, and she had different ones in there, and [I was always -- ]
Fancy that, yeah, that's interesting, yeah. But when did she study with your teacher?
In -- while I was in high school.
In Dallas?
In Dallas, Texas, yeah.
She went and asked for lessons or she knew with the church?
Yeah, she went to him for lessons. He was a good voice teacher also.
That must have been interesting. She
was musical, then.
Yeah, she was musical in that part.

Yeah, she did, she had a very good voice.
Did she?
Yes, she did.
Oh, that's very nice.
And --
Oh, well, that;s interesting. Well, that's good. So that entitled you to have this quartet.
Oh, yes.
Well, then, would you say, Gus, that you were a little bit of a leader then, in the sense that you organized it, you got it together.
Well, yes. Well, the group was together, but I got to be the leader of the group.
Oh, I see.
We used to be on the streets, singing, one of those things.
Did somebody pass the hat or something?
When beer first came in, -- not the first time, but when Prohibition came, --
Sure.
Well, we used to go around singing,
at these little places, they'd have little stands. And guys would come and throw us money and give us money and like that.
Yeah.
But we had a program -- we were in school, I was going to Sumner Junior College and some of the rest were going to high school.
Yeah.
Well, we had to be at this radio station. We had a program for "The Store without a Name."
Really?
That's the name of it, "The Store without a Name." And we would broadcast every morning. And we'd imitate the Mills Brothers.
Yeah, yeah.
That was our big thing.

I was doing the bass.

Right, right, sure.
Well, every morning -- and you'd fit this in with going to school?
We'd have to be there, like -- we had to be at school at 8:00, but our program came on around 7:00 in the morning.
It did?
And we had to get down there, real fast to get -- we did a 15-minute thing every morning.
What did you get paid for that?
Oh, we got about $25, like that. A man.
You did? That's good pay.
Yeah, that's what I know, sure.
How about that?
Yeah, that's right. That was The Store Without A Name.

No, not that long. We did it for About a couple of months.

Oh, sure, we had a lot of new numbers.
A repertoire.
A repertoire. We sang the numbers the Mills Brothers sang, we had our own tunes and all like that.

Oh, yeah.

Yes.
They were beautiful. I don't think any quartet had ever topped them, do you?
Not for me.
Not for me, either. I thought they were marvelous.
They --
They swung, --
That's right.
And they had that --
They still swing, the three of them now.
Yeah. And they had those beautiful voices and that blend.
Sure.
Mellow sound, wasn't it?
And that was like -- we went to the theatre, the Main Street Theatre, to get on at the theatre. We had the uniforms and everything.
Oh, you did?
And something happened, we never did get it. They got a bigger act.
Yeah. Something body cut you out.
Yeah, that was it.
No amateur shows? You never --

The only show we did was Vine Street Variety, and that was with -- and I did that with Jay McShann.
Is that right?
Right.
Well, then we're jumping too far ahead.
That's ahead.

Well, let's go back to --why did we -- we were talking about Lloyd Hunter. How did we get -- how did you happen to remember that you had the quartet? Oh, because you sang. You said, what were you going to do? Here these guys were all drunk.
Yeah, that's right. And so he could get a drummer, that's what it was.
Oh, I see. But he couldn't get a bass.
He couldn't get a bass player.
Yeah.

Fancy that.
How to the bass and everything,
really.

I know, like [Braud] used to do.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah.

I remember Lunceford.
Right.
Yeah.
You know how fast that was.
Yeah.
And then it had that bass solo in there.
Yes, that's right.
My fingers was bleeding. I had blisters on them, and so I had to wrap my fingers in tape and all
like that. That's really awful, isn't it?

That's right.
How long did it take you to where you could get out of pain?
Well, after I put the tape on, I noticed I could -- I didn't feel it so bad.
Yeah.
And so I just kept using the tape.
Yeah, until you got your fingers --
And started taking it off and started playing.
Yeah. Did you enjoy it?
Yes, I enjoyed it. I like bass, but --

Oh, I see.
But I would hit the right notes, each
time I played.
Yeah.
I would know how to read.
You'd use your wrist to get to it instead of your fingers.
Instead of my fingers, and I would slide up and down.
Yeah.
Even Ramey plays that way now sometimes.
Does he? Yeah.
One of those things.
Yeah, yeah.
But I stayed with Lloyd for quite a little while. All of -- almost all of '56.
What?
I mean, not '56 -- '36.
I was going to say.
1936. Sorry about that.
Well, --
And then I left.
You didn't tell me who was in that band. Do you remember who was in Lloyd Hunter's band, or any of the people?
Jimmy Bythewood was tenor player. A fellow named McKinley was the guitar player. Byron --
Little Byron -- Jimmy Byron was trombone.
Well, that's good.
Jimmy Cole was the trumpet player.
That was what, a 12-piece band, in sections, wasn't it?
Yes, it was.
Who was writing for it?
Well, they had a lot of the guys in it.
Oh, a lot of the guys could and did write wrote for it.
And Lloyd did a lot of arranging, too.
Was-he a piano player?
He was a trumpet player.
Oh.
He was a trumpet player.
Good trumpet player?
He was a good trumpet player.
Was he?
He didn't get anyplace because he had a good band, and we cut Nat Towles' Cole's band --
Nat Towles' Cole's.
Right.
Now we've finally gotten there.
And -- because Nat had a good band, and his arranger would sound like Lunceford's, see. And all

the good musicians, but his drummer was weak. And I had gone back to playing drums with Lloyd, see. And Lloyd had gotten another bass player. So his drummer didn't cut the mustard, as they say. He was the weakest guy in the band.
What did Nat Towles play?
I think he played saxophone, but he would always front the band.

Well, you know what I'm thinking, Gus? I could be wrong on this, but you know I said that Lawson's band in Dallas, that they sent for, and I sent to you they sent for Nat Cole. I wonder if I'm not wrong, and they sent for Nat Towles.
They could have sent for Nat Towles.
Well, wait a minute. Nat Towles' band came out of where?
Well, it was from Texas.

Yeah, well, what I'm thinking is that Nat Towles came up and fronted the band I'm talking about, Lawson's band, in Dallas. And that became Nat Towles' band. Or maybe it became the second band he had or something.

Well, I don't know about the second -- the second band? See, now, when I met the guys in the band, even Henry Coker was playing trombone in the band, and one of the trumpet players was Walter Duncans, which we all went to school together. We grew up together. And the bass player
was from Dallas, and his mother was a music teacher. Buddy Tate was in the band. Did I tell you?
No, you didn't, but --
But he was in that band.
And this was about in 1936?
It was.
'35 or '36? So, really, it was pretty well a Dallas band, wasn't it?
It was.
Yeah.
I had that here a few minutes ago. I'm trying to see all the guys that were in that band.
Yeah.
It was a new band.
Yeah.
A bus, a sleeper bus.
Oh, they did?
Oh, yeah.
He could front the band pretty well, couldn't he?
Oh, yes. His band was really sharp, too.
Yeah.
Good arrangements, good musicians, where a large band had -- he had good musicians, but they were kind
of raggedy, like.
Well, if you say they drank a lot, they weren't that -- there wasn't that same band spirit or something.
Well, they'd have the spirit until they would drink so much.
Yeah.
Like, as we were talking about that, I was playing bass in the band. And we left and went to Pipestone, Minnesota. I think that was Minnesota. Yeah, it was, Pipestone, Minnesota.
Yeah.
And we played out in some field, like, where everybody came in from different -- little towns.
Yeah.

And it was hot. And so this guy brought up a bucket of water with ice in it, and then came and poured a whole gallon of just straight alcohol in there. And they began to drink that alcohol and that water, and they got drunk. I'm playing the bass, and the band began to sound bad, because they were missing notes and couldn't play their horns.
Yeah.
And I got mad, and I started cussing out Lloyd Hunter and all of the guys that was drunk. And I

And I told them, him, and everybody else they were fired. And I fired Lloyd, the leader of the band, that night. And he said, 'Okay, well, I'll just take my horn and go.' And he packed his horn up and walked out the door, and got outside, and it struck him that that was his band, and I fired him. And he came back in and said, 'You can't fire me, I'm the leader of this band.' I was the youngest thing in the band, really. And I fired him. And then he came back in, they finished their gig, and he started thinking about it. He said, 'You fired me out of my band. I've never had nobody to fire me out of my band.'
That's very funny.

But they just got on my nerves. I couldn't take it, see. So -- but I got even. I got drunk one night. I'm playing the bass, and so I said, 'They going to get drunk, I'm going to get drunk with them.' And we played this town in Nebraska. And it was in a dance hall, see. We was playing dances, anyway.

And I got drunk just before I got to work. And I came in and we started playing, and all of a sudden this whiskey hit me, and my stomach, and I just threw up all behind the bass. And the guy that was giving the dance, he has a white guy, and he came up and said, 'What's wrong, Gus?' I said, 'Oh, my stomach, it's about to kill me. (Unintelligible) He looked at me; I said, 'I

couldn't hold it." He said, "Where did you eat?" I said, "A little old place down the street." Now, I didn't say anything about that. He said, "Don't you know better than to go down there? Say, That place will kill you. Say, Go on out in the bus and get some sleep." He said, "You need something?" I said, "No," I said, "My stomach is all out of order." And I was just drunk, but he didn't know it, see.
And I went out there and slept for about a half an hour, and I came back and finished my gig.
Oh, isn't that funny.
Yeah. I say, --
Isn't that funny. That was the first time you ever let anything like that happen to you.
Yeah, to get drunk like that. I never got drunk no more after that.
Really?
No, I wouldn't get drunk on the job. But I got drunk that time.
Well, you were made at the guys.
Oh, yes. They would get drunk and I couldn't take it. So I just got drunk with them. If I got drunk it would be after I finished my work.
Yeah, that's right.
I just didn't do that.
No, no.
I didn't do that. I only drank for taste.
get knocked out.
Not to (unintelligible).
No, no, nothing like that. No. So --
Well, how long did you -- how are we doing? We've got quite a while. So what time did you put in with the band, about a year and a half?
Not quite a year and a half.
You just felt you couldn't take it, huh?
Yeah, I wanted to play my drums anyway.
Oh, yes, of course, sure.
I was playing the bass.
Sure.
And so he finally found out that I liked my drums.
Yeah.
So he got a bass player. Debo left, Debo Mills left.
Oh, yeah.
He left and went and joined Horace Henderson.
Did he? Oh, yes, you said that, didn't you? Yes.
And --
Horace really -- that was a territory
Yeah, but he was in New York.
Oh.
See, Horace was in New York when Debo joined him.
But he kept going on the road.
Oh, yes, sure, that's right, sure.
Did you ever get stranded?
The only time I got stranded was in Shelby, Nebraska with Lloyd Hunter's band, and that was on account of a big snowdrift. We were going to Shelby that night, and they had a blizzard, 32 below zero.
And where were you stranded?
Between about --
On the road?

On the road, see. We were about -- well, country miles, we were about eight miles from town, from Shelby, because they were driving, the driver got tired of driving, so we would all switch about, and drive. So I was driving. And the snow was drifting across the highway and you couldn't see as far as from here to that wall.

And I saw this snowdrift right across the road, so I stepped on it and hit it, to go through it, you see. And I hit it and it was like hitting up against a brick wall. I got stuck. We couldn't move. And lucky we couldn't, we couldn't have gone any farther, anyway.
No.
Because the snow cleared away from blowing, and there was about 12 cars ahead of us, see.
And they were all stuck, too.

Everybody -- we had this panel bus, where the heat ran right between your legs, all the way back. It was a pipe ran all the way down inside. We had two rows of seats, two on this side, two on this side, standard the bus.
Yeah.
And so when you get in the bus, you have this (inaudible).
Have this -- yeah.

Heat between your legs, running down there. And if you to sleep and your foot hit that exhaust pipe running through the bus, then you'll smell something. Somebody would say, 'Get your foot off the heater.' And we ended up with pants legs burned and all like that.
But we got out of the bus. So I got out and I said, 'Well, I'll go and see if I can find a house or something.'
Yeah.
I had one of those big camelhair coats that they was wearing during the time.
Yeah.
And so I walked for about two miles up the road, I couldn't find anybody so I came back.
Two miles in all the snow and temperature?
Yeah, 32 below.
Wow.
And so the --
Not a house in sight.

-- baritone player, he put on another overcoat over the coat he had, and he got out. And he started walking and looked like something just cleared the snow, just like that. And then he looked across and he saw a light, way across in the field somewhere. And he couldn't see no more. And he just started walking towards where he thought he saw that light.
And he found this house. And this guy came and got us in one of those sleds.
A black guy or a white guy?
White guy.
For heaven's sake, a human being.
Oh, they were real great out West, really.
Were they?
They certainly were.
Is that so?
Yeah. And they came and got us in this sled.
Honestly?
A wagon with the sled. No wheels, but this man took us to his house and kept us in his house the whole week, all of us, and fed us.
All week?
A whole week, before we could get out.
Oh, I don't believe it.
That's right.
A week before you could get out?

Before we could get out. And when it stopped and we could get into town, he carried us into town in this wagon, sled, to the hotel. And then he wired Omaha for some money, the office, and they sent us some money to pay our hotel bill.
We still didn't play there after we got to the hotel, because of the snow, see. We stayed there three days longer at the hotel.
Gus, you people would have died if you'd been stuck a week in the snow.
That's right, sure, sure. This guy, he came and got us. Anna Mae Winburn was singing with us, at the time.
Well, that's a story, isn't it? Did anybody do anything for that guy?
Yes, we sent him some money. He didn't charge us one penny. But we sent him some money.
Wasn't that a marvelous story?
When we was getting in the --
Well, how could he put up -- how many guys were there, 13?
Thirteen of us altogether.
How could he sleep you?
Well, we just slept on the floor and cuddled up.
Cuddled up, and like that. And the guitar player had blisters the size of a dollar on his hands from frostbite. I just couldn't move my feet, I could just barely move my feet.
By the time you got --
Yeah, when we got to the house.
My gosh.
From the bus to his house, and --
What time of day?
It was late in the evening, see, because we was playing that night, see, --
Yeah. You were nearly there.
Yeah, we were nearly there, see.
Yeah.
And we got stuck, and we just couldn't move.
What do you think happened to those
people in the cars ahead of you?
I don't know. We don't know what happened to them. I really don't know. They got out in time, something like that.
Yeah, yeah.

But this guy, he put us up, fed us and everything. But when he came to pick us up, we were so cold, I was getting in the wagon, the sled, on the sides, and I said, 'Oh, Lord help me,' one of those things like that. And the Lord said, -- I wasn't talking to the Lord. The Lord said, 'Ain't nothing I can do for you.' I said, 'Oh, shut up, I'm not talking to you.' (Laughter.) He said, 'I thought you was talking to me.' I said, 'No.'
Very funny. Was he a funny guy?

Oh, yeah, he was a funny cat. He was a very nice guy. Annamae Winburn had less clothes on that we did, and she didn't get frostbit or anything. And the women can stand the cold, I think, better than men. I'm telling you.
What an experience.
Yeah, that was something else.
Oh, my gosh.
But we --
And so -- but your office sent you money.
Oh, yes.
They didn't leave you in the hole.
Oh, no.
Who was the office, did you know?
I'm going to have to look in this book.
The Kansas City office.
No, no.
Omaha?
Omaha office, the office out of Omaha. That's where the band was from.
Oh, yes, I see. Yeah, fancy that.
So that whole time that band was on the road then, you didn't really play locations.
No.
No.
No locations.
Are we gone?
Yeah, that's it.

Oh, no, not at all. No.
Living in New York, that was very low.
Well, it --

But you must have been getting more

See, I had to pay my room rent out of

Oh, sure, sure. I enjoyed that, you know. And we had a lot of fun. And we had all the jobs sewed up in this town, like, we worked at the club. The club was called KKK. Klub Klee Klo. But we called it the KKK Club, see.

-- the only hotel they had there.

Had it all sewed up. And I was cutting hair on top of that.
Gus, isn't that funny?

I learned just --
Just as you went along.
Just as I went along, by working in barbershops, you know, one of these things.
Fancy that.
See, I used to shine shoes and all like that. All that came up as I came up in Houston, and Dallas and all like that.
And as I say, we didn't really talk about it, but those were Depression days, so that anybody was glad of any work they could get.
That's right, see.
You learned to do anything you could do.
And I didn't mind doing it.
No, that was good.
I enjoyed it.
Well, but I'll tell you, you must have been pretty strong to do all that. I mean, what sort of hours did the band keep?
Well, we worked from -- say, like, 9:00 at night until 2:00 in the morning.
And of course, in a way, you enjoyed it so much.
Oh, sure.
It isn't exactly like hard work.
It wasn't all that hard.
Because you were doing what you wanted to do, anyway.
Sure. I even worked for the Three

Oh, no.
No.

Did you? That was nice, that was good, yeah.

You did?
Her and her husband. So they came to Ottumwa.

To MacShan. Well, did your mother and your stepfather stay on?

No.
So he got off with the bags. She got off first -- he got off later with the bags and he was standing over here. And so I said, 'Where's your bags? Come on, so I can take you to where I'm staying.'

(Laughter.)

No, she didn't let me know, you know?
But she knew what you'd be like, huh?

Well, he has a nerve coming, when he

Well, you know.

Yeah.
So, --

So it was Gene Ramey, myself, Oliver Minor, William Scott, --
What did he play?
Scott?
Yeah.
Tenor.
Oh, yeah.
Bob Mabane on tenor.
Yeah.
And Earl Jackson, alto.
Oh.
See, this was before Charlie Parker.
Yeah, right, right.
And Jay who you know.
Yeah.
We had seven pieces.
Yeah.
And --
You had three saxophones? Three reeds?
Yes. Two tenors, an alto and --
And one trumpet?
And one trumpet?
Who was?
Oliver Minor. Little Piggy.
Oh, I see.
And myself and Jay.
Oh, that was a good --
And we had a singer with us, too. His name was Coleman -- Joe Coleman.
Oh. Well, who was writing for that, three saxophones and a trumpet?
Hm?
Who was writing?
William Scott.
Oh. I see.
He's a Good arranger, a very good arranger.
And so that little band must have swung.
Oh, it was a swinging little band.
Was that the best band you'd been in,
For a small band?
Yeah.
To me, yes.
Yeah.
Yes, very much so.
Jay -- you know --
Spec's band was very good. It was very good.
Oh, it was, yeah.
We had the three saxes in and that made it much better.
Yeah, that's right. Because Jay McShann's image is not truly himself, because he really got an image as a blues man.
Yeah.
You know what I mean?
Yeah.

Because -- he explained to us, because of this record session with Dave Capp and Dave Capp kept saying, 'Guys, I can't sell this stuff.' And he had these beautiful arrangements, and he kept saying, 'I can't sell it.' And they said, 'Do you know a blues?' Jay says, 'Yeah.' And he tells me that when the session came out and the blues sold like mad, every time he wanted to do something and he had Walter
Brown with him --
Walter Brown?
And so he got that image as a blues man. And his piano playing, you can hear there that he is much more than that.
Oh, yes, he used to play different than just the blues.
Yes.
He would play just like Basie and --
Yeah, he liked the jumps drums.
That's right, that's right.
He said himself, he never associated the blues -- himself with the idea of that he liked the blues, but...
No, he did not. He really didn't.

And then, afterwards, when he set himself to study some more, and I don't know whether you've heard some of these latest -- he made a record in Canada. One was a solo piano record and another I think he made with Buddy Tate. And --
I have the one with Buddy Tate.
You know, and he has some beautiful little classical overtones and under tones and all kinds of pretty things that he works in there.
That's right. We used to have little sessions at the house where we stayed in Kansas City.
Whose house?
Where Jay and I stayed.
Oh, you and Jay stayed in the same --
We were rooming --
Oh, you were? Rooming together?
Yes, yes, we roomed together.
For heaven's sake.
Yes, that was on Park Street, Park Avenue, in Kansas City.
Yeah.
And we'd have jam sessions between the fellows, all the fellows would come over to rehearse. Then we'd have the jam sessions.
No kidding. And then would you be out on the street a lot, at night, to see everybody and everything?
Oh, sure. That was all the time. Sure, that was it.
Was anybody drinking heavy or --
What, in our group?
Yeah. Mostly --
No, not drinking heavy.
Just enjoying yourselves.
We were just enjoying ourselves. One of those things.
Yeah.
Earl Jackson, he would get pretty
juiced at times, but not enough to mess up.
No.
See.
Everybody was wrapped up in the music.
Right, that's right.
Yeah.
If we did get kind of juiced, nobody knew it, nobody but --
But yourself.
-- the guys in the band.

That's right, yeah. I can't remember who -- I just can't remember who it is, it'd make you laugh, I know. I don't think it was Gene Ramey who told me. Somebody said, talking about Jay and said Rich, what kind of guy he was, and said, if you needed some help, you were in a real bad way, tell him a terrible story about how bad off you were, and he'd be real upset for you, he'd say, "Well, let me see," and put his hand in his pocket and bring out a dollar.
(Laughter.)
he may not have been like that then, and that was something he learned to do I don't know, (unintelligible) when he was a band leader.
That's when he was in bad need of a drink or something.
Yeah.
Well, the only one that really drank a lot
was Jay.
Yeah. And they called him Hooty.
Yeah, we'd give him the name Hooty,
see.
Why did you give him the name Hooty?
Because he was always drunk at one time. (As a Hoot-owl)
Yeah?
I used to have to take him to work and put him in the tub there, because I stayed in the same house he stayed in. And I could have been staying home in Kansas, but I stayed in Missouri.
Oh, I see.
We were working out there in Martin's on the Plaza, --
Yeah.
-- and he would drink with his friends and he would get drunk, see.
Yeah. Before going to work.
Before going to work. And I'd make him go to sleep and had to wake him up and put him in the shower there, and tub, and get him so he could play his job.
Isn't that funny? Yes, right.
But --
So the kind of leader he was, he wasn't
any drag leader, he didn't throw his weight around too much.
Oh, no, he never did that, never.
And he never has, has he?
Never has, no. He's always bee an --
Easy-going.
-- easy-going guy, and you couldn't find a better guy than him.
No.
Not because I played with him, just telling you how it is.
Oh, yes. How everybody feels about him.
Sure, yeah.

And he used to go home and raise hell with his wife. And I'd take him home. I know he was drunk, we'd get off of work, we'd go by and he'd get drunk and he'd go home and start raising hell with his wife. And I'd say, 'Well, I'm going out,' and he'd say, 'Now, wait a minute, don't leave me, don't leave me.' He'd say some words, and he'd know he shouldn't say them. And if I leave, she's going to jump on him. And he wanted me to stay all night there.
I said, 'No, I'm going home. I'm going to leave you here. You're talking.'
(Laughter.)
That's funny. Did you say he called you 'W'?

Yeah. I don't know why he got that, but he called me "W.W." And he always had different little names for different ones. He'd call me W.W. "Hey, W.W.," one of those things. And then I'd -- I don't know why, but he just give me that name, W.W.
(Laughter.)
That's funny, isn't it?
But his wife, Abicene, she'd run him around the house and he'd be hollering, "Don't you do that, Abicene, stop it, stop it."
(Laughter.)
"Because I'm going to break your head. And I'd say, "There you go again," and she'd get after him again.
Was that -- like, he's told me something. He said that his wife died a few years ago, three years ago or something?
No, she just died a couple of years ago.
That's right.
No, not that one. This was the one before that.
I see, I see.
Yeah.
Yeah, because he intimated but we didn't get into it.
The one that died is the one that had the babies.
That's right, that's right.
The kids.
And then he went back to Kansas City to bring up --
Well, yeah, they --
I don't know whether he meant they were together or not, but --
Oh, he was in Kansas City, but -- because the girls were there.
Yeah. But was he back with her?
No, no, no.
Oh, he just went back. Because he said that he wanted to see that the girls go through school.
That's right.
But they weren't together.
No.
I see. But this is a first one.
That's his first wife, Abicene, yeah.
How funny, that is so funny.
Yeah, he'd get ready to go out and -- 'I'm going in and whup her head this morning.' And know good and well he wasn't going to do a thing.
But he might get his own head whupped.
That's right. I'd say, "You want me to throw your hat in for you?" "Aw, stop that, W., you know good and well she's not going to do anything to me."
(Laughter.)
That's very funny, isn't it?
She used to get on him, though, being drunk. That was why.
And he stayed that way.
Oh, he was always drunk [at night], but I'd get him up so he could make his job, one of those things. But he wasn't the kind that would really mess up on the job.
No.
Nothing like that.
No, no. Because he's quiet, really.
Right, he had a --
Doesn't get rambunctious or anything.

I had a little Model A Ford, and we would drive up and down the streets, going about ten miles an hour. And he would speak to everybody on the street. That was his thing. "Howdy-do, how are you? You're looking so beautiful today, one of those things."
And I'm sitting up there behind the wheel, driving. "Good evening." Then he would say, "Oh, they say we're the nicest fellows in town."
(Laughter.)
That's very funny.

And I was driving his car one day and I turned my head. There was a car in front of me, and all of a sudden I looked up and there I was. I put on the brakes and skid and -- bam, right in the back of the car. But the fenders -- bumpers hit each other. The guy jumped out of the car and come around, "What the hell wrong with you? Can't you drive that car?" Said, "Don't you have any brakes?" I said, "Yeah, don't you see where I slid?" (Laughter.) He couldn't say anything, he just got in his car and left.
Was Jay still greeting people on the sidewalk?
Jay said, "W., are you drunk?" I said, "No, I'm not drunk. He just had no business stopping like that in front of me." I turned my head and I didn't see him. I just run right in the back of him.
Oh, that's funny.
Yeah.
Well, how long were you with that -- were you guys all together, doing that?
Well, I was with him until I went to the Army.
So you had five years, you remained until
you joined the Army in '43.
Right. I was with him til then.
Well, when did he go in the Army?
After I went in the Army.
Yeah.
He went in later. Bob Maybane went in first. He was the first one in the band to go to the Army. That's the tenor player.
Yeah.
And after he went in, well, we had to get -- we had another tenor player, and so somehow or another, they had been looking for me and I didn't know it. John Tumino had gotten my letter.
Because Jay says they came and handcuffed him on the stand,
Handcuffed him?
Yeah.
Yeah, well, --

He said that letter had been following him all over, and he told me that they had a thing written on it which meant, immediate induction, ICC, or something. And they said, 'Sorry, but you're coming with us now.'
Well, I know that--
Was it like that with you?
Well, they knew we were coming to

Tumino said, Chicago. And John Temeeta say, "You got to go in the Army in Chicago, because they have been looking for you and I didn't let you know about it." I said, "Been looking for me?" I know I got a letter saying I was supposed to go to the Army, one of those things. But I didn't know when.
Yeah.
But when I got to Chicago, I went right Sheridan, on to Fort Sheraton, took my exam for that, if you want to call it an exam. But I got my -- what is it, 15-day furlough, it was.
After they'd accepted you.
They'd accepted me.
They grabbed you.
They grabbed me, you know.
Yeah.
But I knew it right there in Chicago. So I wanted to get in the Navy, see, because I had a friend that played in the Navy. Clarence Trance, he was a trumpet player.
Oh.

But I told them so many tales- some details, that one thing I didn't know, they wanted to know if I had any kind of disease or anything. I said, "Yeah, come to think about it. I think I have syph or something like that." So they wrote it down, see. And so after everything was over, I said, "I'd like to go in the Navy." They said, "You can't go in the Navy, you had have
syph, one of those things. I said, "No?" so they stamped down- bam-- Army.
The things you don't know, you're not warned of and you don't know.
And -- so I had to take a spinal test for that.
To prove this, yea or nay?
Yeah, to prove it.
But it was too late.
It was too late. It was nothing, nothing. And I said, "Doggone learn it."
You'd outsmarted yourself.
I'd outsmarted myself, see. And the guy said, you had to go through that spinal tap for nothing.
Was that painful?
Oh, yeah, it's painful because they make a little slip it can -- you hit a nerve there and it paralyzes you. But they drew this fluid out and tested it. Nothing.
Oh, Gus, what a shame.

They said, "Now, you lay there for an hour and don't get up." I laid there for about 20 minutes and I went to get up and something went bam right in the head. It was a pain that you get from all those shots, --
Yeah, they'd drawn something from your
head or something.
Yeah, the fluid out of your spine.
Yeah.
And I said, 'Oh, boy, I'll never do that again.' But that was it.
What a shame.

But some guy gave me some pills that they -- before then, they called them Geronimos. It's supposed to make your heart flutter, keep you from going in the Army. All right, I took about three of these pills. And I went before the doctor, taking this exam. He put the scopes on and listening. He said, 'You got the best heart I've heard come in today.' I said, 'Oh, no.' (Laughter.)
Beat really strong.
And it beat real good and strong. Oh, no, not that. They stabbed that on me, bam. Said, 'Looky here, I'm supposed to go to the Army. Oh, me.' So --
Isn't that awful?

-- I did my 15-day furlough, then I came back to Chicago, went in Fort Sheridan. And I was in there until they sent me to Camp Rucker. But I got a Class A pass time I got into Fort Sheridan. I got to go in, see my wife.
Oh, you could?
Yeah. And --
How much time have we got on this, Gus?
Oh, about 15, 20 minutes.
Oh. Well, then, wait a minute, because we're going too far ahead of ourselves. I want to ask you all about that.
Okay.
But before I ask you about that, didn't Charlie Parker join the band before that?
He joined the band when we started the big band.
Well, what year was that?
That was about --
Before the Army?
Oh, yes, before the Army.
Yeah.
About 1939.
Well, you joined in '38, so was it like a year and a half afterwards or something like that?
No -- what, the Army?
No, the big band.
Oh, the big band was started around '39, I thought.
Oh, I see.
Because -- either '39 or '40.
Yeah.
Because we were in Central Plaza.
Oh, I see.
Central Ballroom.
Oh, I see, I see.
John Tumino.
Oh. Did he own the ballroom?
Yes, yes, yes.
And then he became your manager?
Uh-huh.

Jay's manager. Well, Jay said -- he talked quite a lot about that. He said that he'd heard Charlie on the street somewhere, you know. He said, 'I've never heard this guy before,' but he had heard Bird before, -
Yeah, in Kansas City.

He said, 'What have you been doing?' He said, 'Oh, I've been out on the road, and I've been woodshedding.' So what did you all think when he brought him into the band? Did you think to yourself, 'I've never heard that before?'
He was a good alto player. See, but before he got to be good, they wouldn't let him play anyplace.
Oh, you saw him around those days.
He was --
Ross Russell wrote about that in that book of his.
They wouldn't let him go on --
They wouldn't let him get up on the stand.
Wouldn't let him go up on the stand. But he went in the woodshed, and when he came out, he came out and blew everybody off the stand. He didn't care nothing about nobody.
Yeah.
See, and he just --
And what he was blowing, people hadn't heard that.
Even with Jay, when we'd have jam sessions, we would play this number in five or six different keys, what we call chromatic.
Yeah.
We'd start B-flat --
You'd modulate into the next.
Yeah, just take a half step.
Yeah, like C, C-sharp and all that.
Yeah, right, D and D-sharp and so on, yeah.
And that's the way he used to --
So he'd get all that experience, playing all those keys.
Right.
Yeah, which he loved, didn't he?
Even McShann had to figure out these keys himself.
Yeah, to transpose, yeah.
And Charlie was just running all through them. All the guys in the band, they would do the same thing, trying to keep up with him.
Yeah.
But Bird, he didn't care what he played, what key he played in.
And he liked to take those tempos. Did he want to pick it up all the time?
He liked the tempos.
Yeah.
Oh, sure, he liked fast tempo, and sweet numbers, he could play those, if he wanted. I did have records one time that we made in Wichita. What's those -- acetate records?
Yeah, yeah.
Plastic lined?
Yes.
I had some records we made. I wish you could have heard them.
Gus, that's such a shame because the band wasn't recorded like that, was it?
No, well, the guy came in --
The band came in, the record bands is what they had, isn't it?
The guy came in and would make these records.
Is that right?
And play them back for us and give us some records, one of those things.
Yeah.
And so he gave me a couple of them.
Yeah.
And I'm telling you, my stepsister, she messed them up and left them in the sun, even, and they got warped and all like that.
Oh, wow.
But I wish you could have heard the band on these records, with Charlie playing. He played altogether different than he does now -- than he did then.
Yeah. Jay was saying. -- he said for his money, he played his peak, that he was the greatest.
That's right.
Coming into it, he was doing his own thing, but he had all that background --
He certainly did. And he -- and when he went to New York, then he changed his style again, one of
those things.
That's right.
But I liked him better when he played with Jay.
Yeah.
The way he was playing his alto.
Yeah, yeah.
I'm telling you, But he really played his alto. He knew what he was doing.
Yeah.
His tone was different.
Yeah.
And when he got to New York, then he got on this bop kick.
Yeah, yeah.
Everybody tried to play like Charlie.
Yeah, right.
And we were in the Savoy Ballroom, and we did "Cherokee," and it was up there fast. (singing).
Yeah, yeah.
And we swung that place to death.

McShann said something about -- that they were on the air from the Savoy and that the announcer was going to quite a hip guy or or something, and then you got started, whether it was "Cherokee" or what, went through the whole half
hour.
Sure did. Really did.
And stretched it. The guy said, 'Let him go, let him go.'
That's right, sure did. And we really swung that place.
Another thing Jay said about that was that you really had some battles there, that --
Oh, yeah, we had to battle each band that played on that side, you see.
:Yeah.
When we came to New York, we were late getting there. We were supposed to have been there at 5:00 that evening, to open up.
At the Savoy.
At the Savoy. When we got there, it was around -- almost 9:00. Lucky Millinder was playing. He was on the stand, he had stayed there because we wasn't there.
Yeah. So they were salty, huh?
And we didn't know whether we were going to play or not, because we were late, see.
Yeah. And for the first time in New York. For all of you.
The first time in New York. Everybody was mad with us, see. So we got up there on the stand, you know, and started playing, when we got up there. And Buchanan,

he was mad, and he's rolling his eyes. When we started playing, the floor started jumping, it was jitterbugs and everything. They was swinging back, and Lucky Millinder was on the other end and he was playing all types of tunes, trying to -- a fast one and slow one --
Try to find that --

Trying to find that beat. And we stayed in one tempo, all night long. And when we finally got intermission, Buchanan called us over and just ate us out. And he was thinking about letting us go, but he said, 'You get back on that stand and don't you come off, till it's time to close.' And we had to play all the way through when we got there. And we played and they started jumping. Kept that same tempo. But we outswung everything that was up there that day.
Yeah.
We were afraid. We were afraid, you know.
Yeah, well, all you have to do is really flop once --

We didn't change clothes. We come around with -- had on these clothes. We didn't get a chance to change into uniforms and all. We didn't have that blue coat and brown pants or something, whatever it was. But we just got up there like we were and played.
Yeah.
See, the cars broke down, so that made us the reason we was late.
Well, those things happen and it isn't anybody's fault.
Yeah, but we should have been there.
Yeah.
One of those things.
And, I mean, --
We had to buy new tires. John Ventura had retreads on one of the tires, and they all blew off, and we had to buy new tires. And -- we were just late.
Coming into New York for the first time.
First time in New York. And Lucky Millinder and those guys called us the Western Dogs. And we swung them off the stage.

Jay made me laugh because he said that Buchanan is such a -- maybe not that night, but the night after or something, said to Lucky, 'Come on, and I'll introduce you to McShann or something.' Lucky said,--
He didn't want to meet him.
Forget it, or something. 'I can meet a guy like that any time. I'll see him tonight, or something. And that the band swung them right off the stand.' And Lucky
McShann "You come out with me."
(Laughter.)
Lucky was jumping all over the stand. He was a good front man.
Yeah. He was a good conductor...
Good front man.
Because he had that smile on his face, and -- He jumped down off

with his little box in front of the bandstand and waving his hands. And the band was swinging, but we were afraid, and we just had to do something. And everybody was glad when we got back on the stand, because Lucky was playing the fast ones and everything. So when we did start playing fast tunes, that was it.
Yeah.
See, but we kept just a good bounce all the time.
Yeah.
Good bounce. Just the jump just going.
That's right, just a good jump.
Yeah, yeah.
And the musicians, they all came over to us. They was glad to meet us, one of those things.
Yeah, yeah.
"What happened? How come you was late?"
And we told them. " The tires blew out, we almost had to put a new motor in and all like that.
Yeah.
Which we did. And that's the way it was.
The Western Dogs.
Yeah, called us the Western Dogs, yeah. These Western dogs coming in here, --
(End of Side One.)
Okay. Oh, yeah, that's right. Well, now, Gus, we talked about the fact you were inducted, but then we dropped it and went back about Bird, so let's go back to there.
So they had you, in the Army.
Yes, I was inducted at Fort Sheridan.
Yeah.
So I stayed about ten days in Fort Sheridan, and then I was sent to Camp Rucker, Alabama. And --
Oh, boy.
And I got in the 215 Army Band there.
Oh, so you did have a little luck
then, there.
Yes.
That was good.
So --
Had you been in Alabama before on the road or anything?
Oh, I played --
You'd done a road tour in the South.
Yes, I did a road tour through that way.
Yeah.

But when I got to Alabama that night, they met me at the station, and I was the only one to get off the train about 3:00 in the morning, and one of the sergeants that picked me up was grumping because he had to get up and drive all the way into Ozarks, it was. To meet the train, to pick me up.
So we drove back to the camp there, and when we got there, he put the lights on in the barracks, and everybody started grumbling because the lights came on. And --
You were making a good entry.

And so they showed me to the place I was supposed to sleep, which was one of the bunks right on the side of some of the other fellows there. And had one little fellow in there, was peeping out from under the blankets there. Only thing wrong with him, he was kind of funny in a way there. He peeped out and said, 'Owee, look who come into the camp.'
(Laughter.)
Was he next door?
No, he wasn't next door to me, no. He was way down in the middle of the barracks. I was on the end up there.

But, anyway, one of the soldiers got up and fixed the bunk down for me and everything. And told me I didn't have to get up in the morning unless I wanted to because I didn't have to make reveille or anything like that, which was great.
Yeah.
And--
Was this an integrated company? It wasn't right back then, was it?
No, it wasn't, no.
That didn't happen until after the -- about '45 or something, or '44 or something?
Something like that.
It was Eisenhower, I think, passed a regulation or something.
Yes, it was. But I integrated the band when I got there.
Oh, did you?
That's right.
That was good.
And my first sergeant was Joe Comfort. Maybe you know him. The bass player, he used to play with
Well, I do know him. I have --
-- Harry James' band all the time. And he also played with Ella Fitzgerald while I was there.
And I think he's around New York now, isn't he?
No, he's in California.
Oh.
He's in California.
Is he?
Yes.
Maybe I heard Barnet talking or something.
Yeah, he played with Charlie Barnet, too.
Fancy that.
Well, he was my first sergeant.
Well, that was a slight mercy, wasn't it?
And so --
He dug music.
Oh, yes, yes, sure. Everybody in the band was a good musician, most of them.
Who else was in the band then? Anybody else that you knew?
Only one guy named Williams that I
really knew. I met him because he saw me with MacShann's band, see.
Oh, yeah.
And he was a tenor player.
Oh. Did Joe Comfort -- did he know who you were?
Yes, Joe, he knew who I was.
Oh, well, that was nice, wasn't it?
And he had saw me before. One of those things.
Yeah. That was nice. That was very good.
So --
Because MacShann didn't get to go into any bands or anything, did he?
Not that I know of, but he was there --
Special services, wasn't it?
Special services. I don't even see why they took MacShann because he had such flat feet.
Well, that's what he said.
His feet really gave him trouble.
He said, when the doctors -- after he'd been in about nine months and the doctors told him, they said, 'My God, how did they ever take you?'
That's right.
But he said that they never probably would have taken him if he hadn't been followed all over with that call and they got mad at him, and would take him if he was half dead.
Well, --
Well, you know how the Army is.
Could have been like that.
Yeah.
He played for all the officers and things like that.
Yeah, that's what he said. Well, listen, Gus, so that wasn't -- you weren't too appalled, then. It wasn't too terrible.
No, that wasn't bad at all, you know?
Yeah.

Because -- only thing that got me was, I found out that when you play for the officers or noncom in the Army, you wouldn't get anymore than about two dollars for playing. And so I said, 'Well, I'm going to break this up if I can.' Which I did.
How?
Well, the Eighth Army, before they shipped out to go overseas, --
Yeah.
They went to Japan.
Yeah.
Well, we played a dance that night, and one of the sergeants wanted to know if he could get a six or seven piece band to play for the noncoms, before they leave. They were having a dance.
Yeah.

So I said, 'Yes, I'll see that you get a band.' And when he asked me how much I charged, then that's when I raised the price on the Army. So I told him it would be eight dollars a man, and two dollars for every hour overtime.

And so he said, 'Okay, that's fine.' Just like that, see? So when I got back to the barracks, I told my CO, I said, 'They want me to bring a seven or eight piece band over and they want us to play. But I'm getting eight dollars a man.' And so my CO said, 'You can't do that.' I said, 'Well, they said they would pay it.' I said, 'If you don't say nothing I'm not going to say anything.' So he said, 'Well, if they don't pay it, don't look for it.' I said, 'But they're going to pay it, and they're going to pay for overtime, too.' Which they did. They paid us just like I said. We played about two hours overtime.
Well, so did that establish a precedent or something?
From then on, they began to pay for
