Well, then, where did Earl reach you?
I joined Earl in Chicago.
Well, he wired you or something?
Yes. I happened to know some of the guys in his band, anyway.
Well, who? Budd?
Well, I knew Bud Johnson and I knew the other alto and clarinet player.
Scoop?
Scoop Carry.
Yeah.
Yeah. And Scoop had heard me play and he told him about me.
Well, now, Diz and Charlie weren't with him then.
Oh, no. No. They came afterwards, I think it was. What year was --

Well, I'm just trying to think. Just one second. Worked with Earl Hines and Cootie Williams until joining Basie in late '49. When they were with Earl, the recording ban went into effect and there were no records at the time. Time when Bird and Diz were playing with Earl, that was never on wax.
No. Well, you know, Earl Hines made some records. I was in the band when he made some records, too. And these records never came up. When I first joined him band.
Yeah, those are the -- that's the famous session no one ever found.
He had violin --
Not Ray Nance.
No, he had three violin players in the band on this session. See, and it was a good date.
Wasn't it?
And I don't know what happened. They never did come out, they never did come out.
That's funny.
They didn't get the money. I even asked Earl about that the last time I saw him.
Is that right?
And --
I should think that was like around '48.
Could have been, could have been.
Yeah.
Let's see, '48. Could have been.
Because you joined Basie in '49. So this says.
No, no, that's wrong.
Is it?
Yes, that's wrong. '49, I didn't --
When did you join Basie, then?
No, because late '47, the last --
Is that when you joined Basie?
Yes, very late.
That's why you said you were seven years, and it looked like --
On the phone. Okay, no, because that's when I took Jo Jones' place, see.
That's how come it was seven years. Well, this has got a bit muddled, because -- yeah.
No, no, no.
So you weren't with Earl very long then.
No, no, because the band broke up after we came to New York.
That was the last time he had --
That was the last time he had the big
band.
I follow you, I'm sorry, you're right. Now, this, which may not even be right, says that you worked with Cootie Williams -- probably what they're --
Well, I worked with Cootie Williams' small band.
Oh, did you?
Oh, yes.
At the Savoy?
At the Savoy, yeah.
After Cootie broke up the big band.
After he broke up the big band, I --
Well, who else was in that?
Um, --
Was the other trumpet player -- Merrell?
Bob Miller?
Yeah.
Bob Miller, he was in the band. See, Bob Miller used to be with McShann.
Oh, yeah.
See, he used to be in McShann's band.
Yeah.
He was with McShann when we came to New York.
Yeah.
And Leonard Swain was playing bass.
Oh?
Myself, --
Who was playing piano?
(Arnold Jarvis--ed.)
Jarvis.
I don't know him.
He's from New York.
Alto?
No, piano.
Don't know him. What's his --
Jarvis -- oh, what is it, now? I can't think --
I'm putting you on the spot. But it's very hard to put a name to everybody you know.
Well, I know his first name was Jarvis.
Yeah, well, that's all right. If I need to find out, I can find out.
And we had an alto player. I saw his picture in here somewhere. The name, too. (Rupert Cole--ed.)
Oh. He was, like, taking Cleanhead's place, huh?
Yeah, just in playing, yeah. He didn't sing. Because Bob Merrill was doing the singing.
Yes, that's right.
See.
That's right, yeah. Was Cootie doing much billing? blowing?
Hm?
Was Cootie doing much billing? blowing?
Oh, yes. He blew all the time, every set.
You enjoyed him, didn't you?
Oh, yes, goodness. He had a good group. Good group.
And he's got such a wonderful concept, with so much power and --
We had a tenor player with us, and I can't think of his name, either. But he didn't work out too well, so we got Gator tail Jackson, from Florida.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. And he blew --
Yes. I've got some records there with that on them. I remember we made.
You enjoyed that.
Oh, sure, yeah. Willis Jackson, he was the -- I gave him the name Gator tail.
Did you?
Because he came from Florida, the alligators there.
Yeah, right.
And I used to tell him all he'd eat was
alligator tail and rice, one of those things.
Yeah.
And we had a very good -- he had a very good band.
And Cootie is very particular about drummers.
Oh, yeah. A good strong man.
And there's a a lot of drummers he doesn't like.
No.
He used to get on Sonny terribly, in the band. He used to -- he didn't like --
Sonny who?
Greer.
Oh, Sonny Greer, yeah.
He used to get very mad.
Well, he had a drummer with his big band. I thought sure he was going to take him, but he didn't.
Who was he? Well, it doesn't matter. I know he's very serious about who he's got playing in back of him.
Yeah, he was -- I'll tell you, he --
But Cootie was drinking, wasn't he?
Oh, he always loved to drink, one of those things.
Because he told me that when he finally got ready to quit the whole thing, he just figured that --
This is the trumpet player that was in Specs band, Specs Redd, when I was in Ottumwa, Iowa.
Oh.
Leonard Chadwick.
Oh, yes, that's right. Yes, that's right.
See, he played with the original Blue Devils.
Oh, fancy that. Yeah.
This guy, he's still in Kansas City.
What's his name?
Williams, Ernest Williams.
Oh, yeah.
He used to sing, he was the singer in the band. Let's see, who else -- Doc Ross, Lester Young.
Is that a picture of Lester there?
Oh, yes.
I shouldn't waste the time. Well, listen, Gus, now we got to get on.
Yeah, we got to go ahead.
So you were with Cootie's small band before you went with Earl? Just for a brief time? Or Earl broke up at the Savoy and then you went with Cootie? Which?
I got with Cootie afterwards.
Yeah, yeah. So in other words, before
you joined Basie. What, Cootie? Yes.
Yeah.
Sure.
You were with Cootie.
Well, I had been with Basie, once.
How was that?

The first time I got with Basie, I stayed with him until -- and we went in the Strand Theatre. Now, that's -- I took Jo Jones' place after he took Shadow's place. And so he left and told them to get me to work with Basie.
Jo did.
Yes.
Yeah. Jo was always in your corner, wasn't he?
Well, yes.
Yeah.
And so I went to join Basie, like I said, in '47, see.
Yeah.

And -- the very last part of '47. I stayed with him until we went in the Strand Theatre, and I finished the Strand Theatre. Well, Shadow Wilson came back. He got -- he hired Shadow back into the band.
Yeah, yeah.
And they went in the Royal Roost, right across from the Strand.
Yeah.
And they stayed in there for about three weeks or a month, in the Royal Roost. Then they left and went out on the road.
Yeah.
And so, Jimmy Rushing told me, he said, 'Don't worry about it. I bet you Shadow won't be in the band a good month.' I said --
Did Shadow act up?
I don't know whether he acted up or not. When he left Basie the last time?
Why was it in and out?
Well, they had something going between themselves and so the office wanted Shadow back in the band, that's what it was.
I understand.

And they wanted him to play at the Strand Theatre. I told him no, he wasn't going to play the Strand. I was going to play the Strand Theatre. So his manager, Knowles, they used to call him, told him, -- said, 'Well, he's going to start tomorrow.' I said, 'If he's going to start tomorrow, he's going to have to whip me, and you, too.'

And Basie heard him, and Basie called him in there and told him, said, "He's going to finish this Strand Theatre. Now, you all want him to start over in the Royal Roost, okay, he starts after this job here." So I finished the Strand. And he came in the Royal Roost.

And so when they finished the job at the Royal Roost, they went out on the road. And they were out on the road a week, and he put his notice in and went and joined Woody Herman's band, Shadow. So Basie was left without a drummer. So he told Rushing to call me. And Rushing said, "No, I ain't going to call him." Said, "You didn't treat him right when he was here." And so they got Butch Ballard.
He's a white boy, isn't he?
No, no, Ballard, he played with Cootie Williams' band, too.
Oh, oh.
And so when he got Butch, well, they came back in town, and I was playing with Cootie's band at the Savoy again. And so he came by the Savoy and told me he wanted to talk to me.
Basie did.
Yeah.
Couldn't get somebody else to do his dirty work, huh?
No. He said, "I want to talk to you on
your intermission." So I said okay. So he said he wanted me back in the band because he was going to start a small band. Now, this was 1950, when he started the small band, see.
So I said, "Well, that all depends on what you're going to pay."
: The bread.

Yeah, the bread at that time. Well, the guys wasn't getting that much, anyway. So he said, "Well, I'll give you $125 a week." I said, "Uh-uh." I said, "No, thanks, anyway. I'm working here at the Savoy with Cootie's band, anyhow, so -- and I just turned around and walked away. And he said, "Well, wait a minute, now," one of those things.

And so he came back and he said, "I'll give you $135." Well, that -- I know what the guys were getting in the band. They weren't getting no more than $125. See, I knew that. So that was ten dollars more than the rest of the guys.
: Yeah.
So I said, "Well, I'll let you know, just like that. And so after that, he called me up and he said, "Well, what do you say?" I said, "Okay, I'll make it with you." And he started the small band.
Now, when he started the small band, he didn't have Freddie Green with him. He left Freddie Green out.
: I didn't know there was any time when Freddie wasn't there.

Oh, yes, Freddie was out of the band. I said, 'Where's Freddie Green?' He said, 'Well, I got this job in Chicago and I booked just for a small band, six pieces.' I said, 'Man, you better get Freddie Green back in this band,' just like that. And we made the job in Chicago, at the Brass Rail. And Freddie wasn't with us. It was me, Clark Terry, Jimmy Lewis, Buddy DeFranco, Bob Garth.] He's a tenor player.
Who was the bass player?
Jimmy Lewis played bass. And Basie played that -- we were in there for about a month. That was all.
That doesn't sound like much, does it?

Well, it sounded good, but not to me because Freddie wasn't there for that rhythm for me. We sounded good, I'll tell you that. It sounded good. But I missed Freddie Green. So we came back to New York --
You and Freddie were good pals anyway.
Oh, we were good pals, you know?
Yeah.

And Freddie said, 'Man, tell that man to hire me back in the band.' I said, 'Yeah, I told him already,' one of -- He said, 'You kidding?' I said, 'No, I told him to get you back in the band,' just like that, see. He said, 'All I do is dream about that band.' Which I'm quite sure he did, see.
Of course, it's like his whole life.
And so, when we went out again, Freddie
was back in the band. We had the seven pieces, see. And this time we had Waddell Gray with us, playing tenor. And Clark Terry, myself, Jimmy Lewis, Freddy Green.
What kind of blowing was Clark doing at that time?

He -- Clark can play any way that you like for him to play. He even played like Louis Armstrong, on -- four or five numbers, and just knocked Basie out. Basie didn't know he could do it like that. But he did. And he was just a versatile guy. He's a good trumpet player, he really is.
Barnett was saying the other day, that's the best. There's nobody as good.
He was a good trumpet player. And as far as playing bop and all that, he played bop better than any of the best of them.
He gets around the horn so fast --
That's right.
And maintains that tone all the time.
That's it. So then we started the big band back again, see.
What year? '51 or --
Yeah, about '52, it was.
Yeah.
1952, because '51, we still had the
small band, and we were -- went to Boston and all like that. We were travelling with it.
Yeah.
And also out in Seattle, Washington. We just travelled all over with the small band, see.
Yeah. It must have suited Basie kind of nicely, didn't it, or do you think --
Yeah, it was a good little group, but he was used to hearing the rest of the brass. I was used to hearing it, too, one of those things.
Yeah, that's right.
And so he said, I think I'm going to get my big band back again, one of those things.
Yeah.
And we used to do a lot of just location jobs.
Yeah, that was --
High Hat in Boston. That was Willard Alexander; that was the William Morris Office, I think.
(Unintelligible)
Yes.
Anyway, it was Willard.
Yeah, Willard Alexander. And we did in Seattle, Washington, like, a week there and all around California and San Francisco.
Did your wife travel with you at times?
No. No. She was too busy having babies.
(Laughter.)
When did you marry?
We got married right after I came to New York.
Oh, oh.
We got married in Chicago, though, but we were going together in New York.
Oh, that's great, yeah. And is that when your first girl was -- your second girl.
No, my first girl. All my kids were born in New York.
Were they? Really?
Yeah, sure. Every one of them.
Yeah. Well, so, okay, so he decided to get a big band.
He decided to form his big band again. And that's when the personnel was changed again.
Well, that's when he got Jaws in the band, I guess.
Well, yes, Jaws was in the band, and --
Neither of the Franks were in the band, Foster or Wes.
Let's see, they were in the band, but
not when we first started. He picked up Frank and West later. I think Frank Foster was in there first, then Frank West, and he had Charlie Fowlkes.
Yeah. He didn't have Bobby Pater.
Oh, no, no, none of those.
That was much later. And he didn't have Marshall.
Marshall Royal? He came in later also. We had two brothers in there. One played trombone and one played alto. And he did a lot of the arranging. Hey, Nell.
What, honey?
Who was the alto player that played with Basie, the real skinny --
Coker? Coker?
No, Coker played trombone. And he had a brother played trombone also. We saw him not too very long ago. He turned out to be a junkie, once.
Well, I don't know, I don't know. No, all right, we'll think of it.
(Recording interrupted.)
That was Ernie Wilkins, and his brother, Jimmy Wilkins. He played the trombone.
Yeah, yeah. And who did you have playing bass?
We had three or four bass players at
one time. Oh, Eddie Jones. Eddie Jones was playing bass.
Yeah, so he had a nice rhythm section.
Oh, yeah, a good rhythm section, a very good rhythm section.
Yeah, yeah. Well, that was good. So is that the band that Basie took to Europe?
Yes, he came to Europe with that band. Marshall Royal was in the band, when we came there.
Yeah.
And I think Jaws was with us, too.
Well, Marshall was straw boss.
Yes, that's right. He was the straw boss.
Yeah. And who were those trumpets, then? Was Ernie -- no, Joe Newman?
Joe Newman was in the band.
And Thad Jones.
There was a Jones in there, a little short cat.
Oh, Jonesie or -- (Reunald Jones--ed)
Jonesie, Little Jonesie. The one that played the sweet trumpet. He's not in the band now. He lives out in California. He's an insurance worker.
Oh, is that right?
And --
(Wendell Culley)
Yeah, there was someone else that took the solos along with -- Sweets wasn't back with the band, was he?
No, Sweets -- no, no, no, not Sweets.
Somebody besides Joe Newman. Afterwards, Joe Newman and Thad Jones were in the band for a long time.
Yeah, Thad Jones came in the band before I left the band.
(Inaudible), weren't they?
Yeah.
Well, never mind, it doesn't matter. Well, so that was like about '52, '53 that you came to England.
Yes, uh-huh.
Well, then you left Basie, it says, 23 December, 1954.
Right.
Why?
I had appendix. I had to go in the hospital.
No kidding.
Yeah.
In New York?
In New York.
Fancy that.
Hit me That night, the 22nd or 23rd, I was
in the hospital. And they had to operate on me that next day.
So that laid you up a bit.
Oh, yeah, I was in there about ten, 15 days.
No kidding.
For Appendix, you know, because when they cut me and raised it up, they bust it.
So you got peritonitis.
No, they caught it just in time. At the time it busted, they put the tubes in there and started running it out.
Mercy. Oh, my gosh.
One of those things.
That was lucky, wasn't it?
Sure was.
Yeah.
The doctor came in, fussing at me because I stopped him from going on his vacation.
That wasn't Arthur Logan.
No, Dr. Green was his name.
Oh. Did you ever have Arthur Logan as a doctor?
No, no.
You know who I mean?
I know who you're talking about. No,
I didn't have him. No, my doctor, he was out in came from the Bronx.
Did you ever know Duke?
Duke Ellington?
Yeah.
Oh, sure. I played with him every time Sam Woodyard wouldn't show up. They'd call me.
I must ask you about that. Don't you love the way Sam Woodyard played, though?
Oh, yeah, sure.
He sounded so good in that band.
He certainly did.
I mean, he'd get high and everything, (unintelligible), but he did suit that band so marvelously.
I think the reason why they called me was because I played with Duke's son.
Mercer?
Mercer.
When did you play with Mercer?
Before -- oh, a long time ago. During the times I wasn't working around in New York, see.
Is that right.
And --
--was Strayhorn with the band? When Mercer was (inaudible).
Oh, no, no, no.
Mercer just had a bunch of kids.
Yeah, he had a bunch of guys he had got together for this band, see.
Yeah.
And I worked in this band about four or five times. And he told Duke about it, and so Duke would call me. And Johnny Hodges would have me on a lot of record dates with him, see.
Oh, really? Now, we haven't talked about that.
Yeah.
Yeah, on those small band dates.
Yeah, they were small band with Johnny Hodges, yeah.
Yeah, beautiful.

Yes, goodness' sake. I loved playing with that guy. And just before he died, I came by the theatre there and said, 'You're just the guy I want to see. I'm making a date three weeks from now.' And he died just before those three weeks. I had a record date with him.

Well, when you got out of hospital, and you were ready to play again, you did a spell with Lena Horne?
Oh, yes. Well, when I got out of the hospital, I think Basie came back into town and Sonny was playing with the band.
Sonny Payne.

Sonny Payne. And they made a record date and I went down and made a session. And not that day but about, I'd say, about a month later I made a session with Basie because something happened. Sonny didn't show up, and I don't know what happened, but he wasn't there. And they was out looking for a drummer, and I just happened to be walking down Broadway, and the valet saw me and said, "Good, just the guy I want to see." And went by Columbia Studio and -- yeah, Columbia Studio.
Yeah.
And I made a date with him.
That was nice. Freddie was mighty glad to see you show up?
Yeah. Everybody was glad to see me.
Yeah.
But --
They've had their troubles, haven't
Yeah, sure.
For a band that relies on its rhythm section.
Yeah, they had a lot of trouble.
Yeah.
But he was a good drummer, though, for the band. He was flashy, good flashy.
So the action wasn't so much on swinging the band as on the show.
Well, Basie basically, liked a lot of flash.
Yeah. Well, he felt it sold.
Yeah, sure, sure.
Yeah.

I know he wrote me while I was in the hospital and said that Sonny was doing a good job, and he think he'd make a good drummer with the band, good flashy drummer, and that he was going to keep him with the band while I was still in the hospital.
Yeah, so --
That was all right.
Well, it's what he felt he required. That may not be what the band felt, but that's what --
No, because it was kind of, as they
say, a dirty -- looked like he waited till everybody got sick or was in the hospital or something like that before he fired them. And even with Charlie Fowlkes. Charlie Fowlkes fell and broke his --
I remember, and was out for ages, wasn't he?
Yeah, and he didn't hire him back. Marshal Royal, when something happened to him, he had to go to the hospital, and he got the other --
In other words, don't get sick.
Well, that was the way it was. Don't get sick, see. But I had always told him that if he felt that he wanted to get another drummer, just let me know, one of those things.
What did you feel about the spirit in the band, as far as the band went? Was it enjoyable?
When I played with them?
Yeah.
Oh, it was fine with me. I enjoyed playing with the band.
But there were cliques and things, weren't there?
Well, I --
Or you didn't have to be aware of them.
They could have had cliques. I'm
quite sure they had a few cliques in the band.
Yeah.
Certain ones that wanted a Sonny in the band.
Yeah.
And which I found out later, it was.
Well, tell me, I'd like to know, if you don't mind saying.
What? No, I don't mind saying.
Who were the guys?

Which was told to me, that, like, even Charlie Fowlkes, he told me Basie that Sonny was the better drummer and the more showman and like that. And then come to find out he was one of the guys that got let out, too.
That's funny, isn't it?
Yeah, it was real funny, you know?
Yeah, that is funny.
But that was all right with me.
Yeah.
Because after that, I did go with Lena Horne.
Yeah. Well, --
George Duvivier called me on that.
Oh, he did?
Yes.
Well, that was nice. That was good. Who else was with Lena? A little group?
Yes, it was just a trio.
Who was the piano player -- Tommy Flanagan?
No, no, no, this was Italian.
A white boy.
White boy, yes.
Her husband. Oh, no, no, no.
What's his name? I can never think of this guy's name. I always have to ask George Devivier what his name is.

But what was her husband's name, the arranger and bandleader? Lena's husband? Some Italian name, wasn't it? Oh, let's not waste time on that. Everybody knows so it doesn't matter. It doesn't even matter who the piano player was. The main thing was, he played nice accompaniment for her.
Oh, yes, he was a good accompanist.
And so how long --
Lenny Heywood, Lenny Heywood, her husband. Yeah, that was her husband.
That's right. And so, was he playing the piano?
Sometimes he'd play, on some numbers.
Oh, I see, yeah.
Behind her.
Yeah.
But he did a lot of the arranging for her.
What was it like, working with Lena?
Well, it was all right.
Was she temperamental?

Not with the trio. The only thing that got me with her, it was little things she would do, kind of snarl in her singing, and I thought she was snarling at me. But she wasn't, at all. It was just the way she put her song over. And that used to worry me. I was thinking, maybe I did something wrong, or something like that.
Oh, really? Yeah. Did anybody tell you --
No, I never did tell anybody about that, see.
Yeah.

But I told Lennie that I had to leave the group because I didn't think I was doing my job, see. And Lennie said, 'What's wrong with you? You've learned the numbers faster than any of the best readers we have. And you're playing the numbers fine. This was in Los Angeles, at the Cocoanut Grove, there. That's where I left them.'
So it affected you that much, that you --

Yeah, I even had pains running across here, and I went to the doctor. And one doctor told me I had heart trouble, I couldn't play tennis. And I didn't believe him. So that same day, I went to another doctor and he took my blood pressure and he said, "What are you so uptight about?" I said, "I'm not uptight about anything." He said, "It's got to be. Your wife leave you or something like that?" I said, "No, my wife is all right."
That's my other girl.

And I said, "So why you asking me that?" He said, "Your blood pressure shows you're uptight." I said, "Are you kidding?" And he said, "Who do you work for?" I said, "Lena Horne." So he said, "You can't be uptight with her." And when he said that, that just --
Registered.
Registered right in my head that that was what I was uptight about. And I went right back and put my notice in.
Isn't that something?
And, really, --
It wasn't anything.
No, it was nothing she had said to me at all. She had never said nothing to me.
No, yeah.
Anything like that. But it was just
the way that she was doing, -- Yeah.
-- and I figured I was --
It made you nervous.
Yeah, I figured it was me.
Yeah.
I'd been with her quite a little while, you see.
And the money was fairly good.
Oh, the money was good, very good. It was good.
Well, did you go to Ella after that?
After that, yes.
Well, that must have been a pleasure, working with Ella.
Well, it was a pleasure working with her, too.
I didn't mean that, but I meant that Ella is such a wonderful musician.
Yes.
That, I mean, it is a pleasure to work back of somebody that can do what she could do.
Oh, yeah, well, she has her little ways, too. She is self-conscious of herself.
I know.
Which is -- she shouldn't be, at all.
She lacks the confidence, and she should have all the confidence in the world.
And, like, she knew she wasn't as pretty as Lena Horne.
That's right.
But she sounded better.
Oh, yeah, nobody is going to sound better than --
No, nobody is going to sound like Ella.
Right.
And Lena had her own thing she does. And what she does, she does well.
Yes.
And she puts it across.
Sure.
She does beautiful, you know?
Yeah, she's inimitable in her own fashion.
Right, see. But you could come up and say, 'Oh, yeah, Lena Horne and so and so and so, you could see that -- you're thinking about beauty, which you wouldn't be thinking about that. And I used to --
Because she'd be very sensitive.
Yeah, she's very sensitive on things like that. And she could see you talking and think you were
talking about her, bad things, which you wouldn't have to be talking about her. And I think she kind of worried herself more, like that.
During her whole career, I suppose.
Yeah, you know?
Yeah.
And I used to tell her all the time, 'Go ahead and sing. Ain't nobody talking bad about you.'
Yeah.
They love you, you know?
Yeah. Yeah, really, it's a lot of modesty in her, because to have the talent she has --
Oh, sure.
A whole lot of people would have thought, 'What can they say?'
Well, that's it.
When I sing like I sing.
Well, that's right, that's right.
You know?
But Ella was always trying to improve, everything she did, she was trying to improve herself.
I know.
And she wanted people to love her.
I know.
And like that.
She's a very conscientious person.
She's beautiful to me, one of those things.
Yeah. But, still, it made for a little tension on the job.
Oh, yeah, it made [Tommy] uptight.
Yeah, because if she's anxious, it made everybody a little uptight.

Just like when Tommy Flanagan, for instance, got with the group. Well, we were playing some club in Cleveland, and -- I think it was the Harlem Club in Cleveland. And this was his first night with the group.
Yeah.
And he was doing the best he could, and she turned around on him and liked to scare him to death. And so I -- I saw it and I just said, 'Turn around,' just like that.
At her?
I sure did.
Good for you.
And, boy, that kind of shocked her, I believe, in a way.
Yeah.
But she got over it. I walked behind her, waiting for her to say, 'You're fired,' one of those things.
But she didn't, and I told her, I said, 'This is his first night and he's nervous and he doesn't know the numbers right then.' The first time he ever played behind her, you know.
Yeah. No rehearsal or anything?
Well, we had a rehearsal, but --
But it's not the same --
It was just right then and there.
Yeah, right.
When he came in, you see.
Yeah, right.
And he did good, you know. But she was uptight, too, you know, at that. Losing her piano player, we called him Lloyd Proper at times, because he talks proper. You know him.
Not Lloyd.
No, his name is not Lloyd.
No, no, I know, but I was thinking --
Not Lou Levy. No, this is a black guy.
Kind of got big eyes.
Not Milton Larkin.
Not Milton Larkin.
I don't mean Milt Larkin. I mean Ellis Larkin.
No, no, no, not Ellis. I'll tell you a little later.
(Don Abney)
It'll come. We'll go back to it.
So --
Well, come to find out Tommy accompanied her better than anyone, didn't he?
That's right. He stayed with her. He's still with her, when she goes out.
Yeah, yeah. And she is a person that really appreciates an accompanist.
Oh, yes, she does.
That does half her work for her, or a whole lot of her work --
I loved working with Ella, I really did.
Yeah. Who was her bass player?
At the time I was telling you about Tommy Flanagan, Benny Moten. He's a bass player.
Is he the son of the other Benny Moten.
No, no, no. No kin whatsoever.
Fancy that.
He was playing bass at the time.
Yeah.
And --
Well, how long did you work on and off with Ella? Did you go out on the road a lot?
Nine years.
I didn't realize that.
Yeah, I was with her clean up to 1965. I joined her in '56.
Well, now, this thing says that you were with Woody Herman in '59.
That was just for a little while, with Woody's small group. And then I went right back with Ella, see.
Well, I never. Fancy that. Well, she must have loved you, Gus.
Well, I stayed with her a long time.
Yeah.
Yeah. I don't know whether she loved me or not, but when I first moved out here in '73, and she played her, well, they sent me a telegram, calling me.
Who, Norman Grant?

Yes, he played with her here in Denver, in '73. And I could have stayed with her, but I was playing with the World's Greatest Jazz Band at the time, which I should have stayed with her, because I went out and made four weeks with it, on the road.
Right then, from --
From here, yeah.
Yeah. Well, so you went all over the world with Ella.
Oh, yeah, that's where I did most all of my travelling, with her. That's where all of my biggest travelling.
So you never played anything but houses of wild enthusiasm.
That's right, that's right.
And Norman handled you very nicely, I think. Everybody travelled very nicely, and --
He's a great cat. I like him.
Do you?
Yes.
He's egotistical.
Well, I guess so.
Who isn't, you mean?
Who isn't? Everybody got their ways, but --
First of all, he appreciates the music. He knows what he's listening to.
He knows what he's listening to. And he know his business.
Yeah.
That's one thing.
Yeah.
He knows his business.
And he does think the artist should be treated just right.
That's right, that's right.
Which nobody else is really in that ball game.
I've never had any trouble with him.
That's not George Wein, is it?
I don't know, I never had trouble with Wein, either, but everybody else has.
Everybody else has, yeah.
But I never had no trouble with him Gran z. or with the Norman Grants.
Oh, well, that's -- I'm not surprised you didn't have --
Norman would say, 'You want this? You want that? Do that, and that's that.'
Yeah.
And no problems whatsoever.
You must have enjoyed it. You and Tommy together.
I did, I did.
It must have been nice, you and Tommy got along nicely, I don't doubt.
Well, --
Not always?
I hate Tommy like I do (Unintelligible) Buddy Tate.
(Unintelligible discussion.)
That's our little thing together. No, we love
each other, honestly. Just like, there's a friend of mine, a trombone player. We just fuss and argue all the time, but we are just like that. We're two peas in a pod.
Trombone player here?
(Unintelligible.)
No, Carl Fontana.
Oh, yes.
Hey, wasn't that sad about Rosalina?
You know Carl, you've heard --
(Unintelligible.)
Yes, it was, it really was. And he made the party here.
Yeah, very nasty.
You never know what's going on in your head.
You surely don't. Because that guy, very extrovert and very happy-seeming guy, huh?

That's right. You take George Du- vivier, now. He's another one of my worst enemies. We used to walk in the studio, and if we see one another first -- somebody first, -- he'd holler out, "Who's playing drums?" And somebody would say, "Gus Johnson." "Gus Johnson? Give me my bass, let me get the hell out of here."
(Laughter.)
If I know he's there and I see him, I say, "Oh, no, no, I can't play with him. Get somebody else, I don't make the gig, just like that. And everybody's looking, "What's wrong
with him? Looky at there, he can't play with him? As good a bass player as George Davivier? " And we still carry on like that.
How funny.
We were Going to California? . . .
Yeah.

And we passed through Denver, I'm driving his car, see. We stop downtown for a light, and we're just arguing. He's arguing about my driving his car. So I told him, "Just get the hell out of my car, just like that. His Cadillac, he gets out and slams the door. "Well, just take your old car and get out of here, " and I'd just drive right on off and leave him on the corner and go around the corner, and he's standing there.

I say, "Hey, buddy, what do you know?" He'd say, "Hey." I'd say, "You want a ride?" He'd say, "I don't care if I do." And he'd get in the car and everybody's looking and saying, "What's wrong with him?"
(Laughter.)
That's funny, isn't it?
We're always pulling that.
And is that what you do with Buddy Tate?
Oh, Buddy Tate, yeah, the brightest -- I call him the Texas Pimp.
(Laughter.)
Oh, that's funny.
His daughter was in New York, out on Long Island. She's out there to listen to the band.
Yeah.
I came up and I saw Buddy, and he's sitting there, and his daughter -- a pretty girl, too, yes, she is.
A pretty girl, I know her, too, yeah.

And I say, 'My goodness.' He said, 'Never mind that. Honey, see that guy? Don't say nothing to him. He's a dirty guy, don't trust him, don't turn your back on him.' I said, 'Who is that? You don't want to introduce me to the young lady? This is my daughter and I don't want to catch you hanging around her.'
(Laughter.)
That's why I don't like him, see.
Cramps your style.
Right.
That's funny.
I can't flirt with nobody. He just messes me up.
That's funny. Well, listen, Gus, all right, so -- oh, yeah. So then, this goes on to say that as well as working with Ella, that you did quite a lot of session
work and club appearances with jazz groups, including regular work with Jerry Mulligan.
Right.
Well, when was that? In the '60s?
Yes, uh-huh.
In New York?
In New York.
Did you go on the road?
Yes, we went out on the road.
Who else would --
Brookmeyer, Bobby Brookmeyer on trombone.
Yeah.
And myself and Bill Crow on base.
Yeah, yeah.
It was just the four of us, you know?
Yeah. Gus, you never -- integration and all that, you never had any trouble of any kind. All went pretty nice?
Not that I know of, not really.
Not a lot of people will say that, either.
I had more trouble with my own group than --
Yeah, fussing and fighting and maybe
in the family, kind of.
Yeah, like that.
Yeah, fancy that. That's nice, that's very nice, isn't it, because not a lot of people are going to say that.

Just like Woody Herman. Well, I played on the big bands, too, see. And I'm trying to -- let's see, I think it was -- about '65, when he went down -- no, 60-something, when Jake Hannah joined the band.
Yeah.
Well, they left and went to Brownsville, Texas.
Oh?
They were going to Brownsville, Texas. That's when Woody got Jake Hannah, because he figured that there was going to be a lot of Jim Crow, you know.
Yeah.
And they were on their way to Houston, Texas.
Yeah.
So he told me, he'd say he didn't want me to feel bad about it.
Yeah.
And --
He figured you things would be ticklish.
Yeah, kind of ticklish. I told him, no, I wasn't going to be ticklish about it. But that's the way -- if you think it's going to be like that, okay. Which at that time was --
Yeah.
He hadn't been down there.
Yeah.

And so, they left and went to Houston first, and by the time they got to Houston, he called me long distance. Nat Pierce called me. He said, 'Man, Woody want to talk to you.' I said, 'Yeah? What's the matter now?' He said, 'He just wants to tell you something that happened.' And so he put him on the phone. And first thing he said, 'Hey, Gus Dick -- now, wait, he got that from a florist we passed by. It was a name, see, and it was another name, Cockburn was the name. And so I would call him Woody Cockburn, one of those things. I say, 'Yeah, Woody Cockburn, what are you saying?' He said, 'You're not going to believe this.' I said, 'Now what's wrong?' He said, 'I get here at the Rice Hotel, in Houston, and my rooms are not ready. And I send for the manager, and the manager came out.' And he said, 'Guess what,' and I said, 'What?' He say, 'The manager is a black man here.' I said, 'Yeah?' I said, 'Well, what's wrong with that?' He said, 'Nothing, but he rang for the bellboy and when the bellboy came up, it's a white boy.'
And I told him about my rooms, and he went right on and got my rooms for me. He said, 'things have really changed down here.'
(Laughter.)
I said, 'Well, can you believe that? I don't believe that.' And he went down to Brownsville, Texas, and he told that things had changed down there. So I said, 'Well, that's the way it is.'
He moved in haste.
Yes, sir. You never know until-you get there. Which I didn't know, either, see. But everything turned out all right.
Yeah.
And I made a lot of dates with him since then, see.
Yeah.
But that's the way it was.
Yeah.
So I never had any trouble.
No, no, yeah. That's -- some guys are hotheaded.
Yeah.
And they're going to jump to it right away before maybe it's necessary, and --
Just like Benny Goodman. I made some
dates with his sextet.
When?
Oh, that was before I came here.
Yeah.
That was after I left --
Was Buddy working with the sextet, too?
Who?
Buddy Tate. I don't know whether --
No, no, Buddy wasn't on this date.
Yeah.
It was somebody -- let's see.
Was it Zoot?
Zoot was on one date. And then it changed and then it changed and somebody else was on another date with him.
Yeah.
But he used to call me quite regular when I was in New York, see.
Yeah, I know it means an awful lot to Benny to have somebody sitting up on drums that takes care of business. I always did, with him, and it sounds understandable, doesn't it?
Like when he went to Russia.
Did you go with him?
No, I made the rehearsals for the band and I didn't go back. Something came up and I didn't
make it.
Yeah.
No. And I made the rehearsals with the band.
Yeah.
Instead Jake Hannah, he made it.
Yeah.
And I went out --
I wouldn't want to be in the position of sitting up on drums for Benny if you weren't pleasing him.
Well, I was surprised. I never had any trouble.
I'm sure you didn't. I'm sure you didn't, because he's really --
On the concerts, and --
No, I know you wouldn't, because --
And his manager told me, he says, 'he likes you, he likes your playing.'
Yeah, I'm sure he does. What he suffered was from guys that didn't really swing, and didn't make him happy.
Well, I don't know, but I heard a lot of bad talk about him, on account of the way he act.
Yeah, he can act very badly.
Yeah, I know.
But if he likes what you're doing, he doesn't act badly.
No, no, that's right.
I'll give him credit for that. It's the music. As a general rule, it's the music with him.
Yeah, no problem whatsoever I had with him.
Well, that's good, that's very good. Well, so -- but Jerry Mulligan, we were saying, so you went on the road with Jerry, too?
Yeah, we went to Europe -- I went to Europe with him.
Oh, you did?
Sure.
Well, what's Jerry like to work with?
Oh, he's a nice guy. No trouble with him, either.
He's Irish.
I know, but he's a nice guy to work for.
That's nice.
And --
And you like the way he blows.
Yes, oh, yeah, I like the way he blows. Only just somebody I really had any worries with was Bob
Brookmeyer.
Oh.

And he would call me Gussie, and I'd say, 'Call me Gus and not Gussie. Don't call me by any other name, see. Just call me Gus.' And he would always come up with this Gussie stuff. And I had to straighten him out over in Europe, see. And so did the bass player had to straighten him out, too.
Who was he?
Bill Crow.
Oh, yeah. Were they buddies?
Yeah, they were buddies, but they had to straighten him out also.
Yeah, yeah. So then they found out what's what.
Yeah, so I had no more trouble with him, see. That's the only time I've had trouble with anybody like that.
Yeah, yeah.

And Zoot Sims and I, we get along like that. We're arguing and fussing with each other, just for the heck of it. It was Zoot Sims and Al Cohen. We were working down at the Halfnote. And Al Cohen came up and said to me, he said, 'It's time to go play.' And I'm talking to Zoot. And I turn around and say, 'Can't you see I'm talking over here?
What do you mean, coming over here and telling me let's go play, and caught him offguard and he looked at me and say, oh, excuse me, one of those things. And we'd just crack up.
(Laughter.)
He's a gentleman, isn't he?
Oh, yeah. And then [that Carter] he'd say, you guys ain't no good. Get on that stand.
That's funny. That's funny, isn't it?
Yeah.
They're two swell guys, honestly.
And they blow, too.
Oh, sure, yes.
And Zoot seems to blow more all the time, doesn't he?
He's blowing better and better.
Isn't that incredible?
Wonderful, wonderful. He's he sure
Wonderful, he sure is.
I'm telling you.
It is, it really is. That's something, isn't it?
He's always getting after me because of my pistol. You still got that big old .45? Yeah, I'm carrying it with me everywhere I go. Because I was on the force there in New York at one time, you know.
No, I didn't know that. No, I sure didn't.
You didn't know that?
When was that?
Oh, it was during the time before I went out, even with Ella, I was on the force. But I didn't let them know about -- I was going out. I was on sick leave quite often.
How funny. How long did you do that, a couple of years?
Oh, yeah. Well, it was more than that.
Did you, really?
Oh, six or seven years.
Is that right?
Six or seven. I forgot about it.
Well, so you know that Gene Ramey talks a bit nuts in a way, gets ideas, yeah.
Sure.
That's something. So Zoot kids you about packing your .45, huh?
Oh, yes, that's the first thing he says when he sees me now. I say, 'It's on my hip back here.' I've nothing on my hip but my wallet.
(Laughter.)
Isn't that funny?
Yeah.
Well, listen, I'll tell you what stage we've got to, when you appeared with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, which was -- of course, Dick Gibson was back of that, wasn't he?
Oh, yes, yes.
Well, how did that happen? I mean, who approached you on that? Bob Zirk or [Zoot] or --
No, it was a bass player, Jack Lesberg.
Oh.
I came down to the Half Note one night and Lesberg came in.
You integrated that band, didn't you?
Yes, I did.
I thought so. So he came in.
No, no, I didn't. They had a clarinet player before -- what's his name? He died.
A black clarinet player?
Yes.
Who did he work with before?
Oh, he worked with a lot of jazz groups in New York. Very good clarinet player. I'll have to figure out -- let's see, what is his name?
Funny. Was he with bands? Big bands?
He could have been. I'm quite sure
he was.
I can't place him. Oh, you don't -- I know who you mean. It's Ed Hall.
Ed Hall, that's right. That's who I'm mean -- Ed Hall.
(End of Side One.)
So, Gus, we're talking now about -- all right, Gus, so now what we wanted to talk about was that World's Greatest -- so Lesberg came in.

Oh, yeah, that's right. And Jack came in the club there. I was playing there, with Zoot and Al Cohen. And so I went over and spoke to him during intermission, like I came over and I said, 'Hey, Jack, where have you been? I haven't seen you in a long time,' like that.

So he said, 'Well, I've been out in Colorado, been playing for a party out there. For a rich guy that has a party every year.' So I said, 'Well, how come you didn't take me with you, just kidding.' So he said, 'Well, he had about four or five drummers. And so he didn't need another drummer.' I said, 'Well, talk him into getting me out there,' just like that.
Yeah.
And he said, 'Well, I will. Cliff Leeman, he's been kind of sick. And maybe something might happen to get you out there.' So I said, 'Well, that's great.'
And then, first one thing and then the other, and I didn't see him anymore after that.

So the next year, I did get a call. And I answered the phone and I said, 'Hello?' And he said, 'Hey, Gus, this is Jack.' I said, 'Yeah, Jack, what's happening?' He said, 'Well, I got you that job out there, if you want it, playing the party.' I said, 'You've got to be kidding.' And he said, 'No, really.' He said, 'If you want to play it, you can play it.

I said, 'Well, sure, I'd like to play it, just like that. And so he said, 'Well, I'll let you talk to Dick Gibson. He'll call you later on. So I just called to let you know. And you might play and you might not,' he said. 'Because Cliff Leeman is ill and if he can't make it, then you'll have to play. But if he can make it, you won't play. But he will pay you anyway.
He wanted you to come out anyway.
Yes, he said, 'And the room is free and food is free. And you get $400 for coming out.'
Yeah, yeah.
I said, 'Well, that's all right with me. I can't lose on nothing like that.'
Yeah, that's right.
And so I went out. I came out here. And I met him.
You hit it off with Dick.
He called me after Jack got finished talking. He called me later, and he told me the same thing Jack had just told me, see.
Yeah.
So I told him, 'Yeah, I'll make it, be happy to make it.' And so I came out, and I played the party, which was set at Vail, Colorado.
Yeah, before they moved it.
Yeah. The first one before then was in Aspen.
Yeah.
But this time it was in Vail. So I got here and met everybody, a lot of my friends from New York and different places. Surprised, to see them all --
To see who's there.
Yeah. Which I was happy that I was there, too.
Sure, that's right.

And so he made out the slip. He said, 'I don't know, maybe you'll get to play, like I said. But don't worry about it, you'll get your money anyway.' I said, 'Well, that's okay. If I play, I play. If I don't, I don't.' Because I knew I was going to enjoy myself, like that.
Yeah.
And so he put me up in one of the
rooms in one of his houses. He had four houses then.
Yeah.
And so we went to Vail and I was listening to the guys, different ones, playing, Teddy Wilson --
Joe Venuti.
Yeah, Joe Venuti. And Milt Hinton was there, and Bob Haggert. They had what they called the giants of jazz, the great giants of jazz.
Yeah.
So -- but Billy Butterfield, a lot of the -- Safransky on bass.
Yeah.
He was my roommate.
Oh, was he?
Yeah. And he didn't make it that night because of the altitude. Safranski. He got very sick.
Is that right?
But it ended up, I played with Teddy Wilson and Milt Hinton, just like that.
Oh, sure.
And everybody loved it, see. And so I've been making it ever since.
The thing was -- I guess Dick realized that you could fall in follow behind anybody, really, more or less.
Yeah. Well, I played with a lot of
groups. Even Boyd Rayburn, I made some dates with him. Sure. Right there in New York. And all different types of bands.
It must have surprised you sometimes, the guys that would call you.
Well, yeah, like, I first met Boyd Rayburn in Chicago, because we followed him into the Bandbox, MacShann's band.
Oh, yeah.
They followed Boyd Rayburn in the Bandbox. And that's when I composed this song, Under the Moonlight Starlight Blues.
Oh, yeah.
And --
You did well with that song, didn't you?
Yeah, pretty fair. I just need someone else to play it now.
Yeah.
The World's Greatest Jazz Band played it. MacShann played it in front, when the first time I did it, Skippy Hall made an arrangement for the big band.
Oh, yeah. And so Mac was the first one to play it.
Oh, yeah.
And I got it on record with the World's
Greatest Jazz Band.
Oh, yeah, you did, huh?
Sure, yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
And everyone that heard it think Duke Ellington wrote it.
Really?
Yes.
No kidding.
I intended for Duke to --
See if you could get Duke to do it.
Yes, he was going to do it for me.
Yeah. That would have been good.
Yeah, I'd love that.
Yeah.
Then Basie never did play it. We later did a rehearsal on it. Ernie Wilkins made a little arrangement. And he didn't do too hot with it.
Well, I remember guys like Bobby Plater saying to me, you know that Basie would say, 'Yeah, yeah, make arrangements on it, and never call the numbers.
Oh, yeah, he would do that, he would do that.
And keep calling the same numbers and never call the number of a brand new number yet.
Uh-huh.
Funny, isn't it? But you hadn't written anything before that, had you?
No. That was my very first thing.
Yeah.
Now, Get Me On Your Mind, that -
Oh.
Hibbler sang that.
With Mc Shan?
Yes.
That was nice. Well, that went over very big, didn't it?
Yeah, that went over great. That was the first one.
Yeah.
And then, "Under The Moonlight Starlight Blues" is second.
Yeah. That's the -- the very title is like Ellington.
"Under the Moonlight --
Starlight Blue" -- yeah, that's kind of Ellington.
They figured it like -- [Ella's] Ellis' arranger, what's his name, little short guy? That arranged for Duke Ellington?
Oh, Billy Strayhorn.
Billy Strayhorn, yeah. They all figured that it was his number, too.
Isn't that something? Fancy that.
Yeah. But -- never heard it before.
Fancy that.
I was sitting at the piano at the Bandbox -- the Music Box, I believe it was, in Chicago. That was right under the Brass Rail.
Yeah.
And just fooling around with some chords, cards.
Yeah.

And the little tune came in my head, and I started picking it out. The bartender over there began to whistle right along with it. And he said, 'What is that?' I said, 'That's a number of mine.' He said, 'Well, I like it, it's pretty. What's the name of it?' So I said, 'Under the Moonlight Starlight Blues,' just like that. And that was it.
Isn't that funny.

And I wrote out the lead and the chords and gave it to Skippy Hall, and he made an arrangement for the band. And he used to play it all the time. And every time Ralph Sutton played it on the piano, everybody liked it.
Isn't that nice?
Right now.
Ella never sang it.
No, no.
She might have sung it, if you'd asked her, mightn't she?
You didn't want to ask.
I didn't want to ask. I didn't think she would. I just had that feeling.
You think?
Yeah. And Benny Carter is supposed to make an arrangement on if, if we go back to --
Japan?
-- Japan this year.
Oh, that's good. That ought to be nice.
Yeah, I hope so.
Yeah. Well, that's very good. Well, anyway, so -- all right, you're up there at Dick's and you're doing this and that. So then what happens with the World's Greatest Jazz Band?
Well, I stayed with them for quite awhile.
Did they -- so you leave the party, and they say, 'Do you want to come to work, or what happened?
Well, no, that -- I stayed here, because -- I believe I did. No, I didn't. I went back to New York.
Yeah.
And so while I was there, the drummer that played with Peanuts was playing drums with the World's Greatest Jazz Band first.
Yeah.
Morey Feld.
Yeah.
He was the first drummer.
Yeah.
That played with the World's Greatest Jazz Band.
Yeah.
See. And so, they came to New York and when they came to New York, well, Peanuts sent for me to Morey Feld's work in Maury Fell's place at -- here in Denver.
Oh.
In his club.
Oh.
And so I was here six weeks with Morey Feld Peanuts Hucko and Maury Fell was with the World's Greatest Jazz Band.
I see.
Morey Feld
But Maury Feld wanted to come back to Denver, and so when he came back I went back to New York.
Yeah.

And about two weeks later, Gibson called me and told me the fellows wanted me in the band. And so I said, 'The fellows want me in the band, just like that.' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'Well, what happened to the drummer that was there?' He said, 'Well, something happened between he and I, just like that. And I said, 'Well, that's your business then, just like that.' Are you sure they want me in the band?' And he said, 'Yes, they want you in the band, that's why I'm calling you.' I said, 'Oh, okay, I'll come out and play with the band.' And that's when I joined the band.
Fancy that. Well, --
Morey Feld
Maury Feld started working back with Peanuts.
Yeah. What's the trumpet player's name?
Yank
Yeg Lawson.
Yank?
Yeah. Did you get along with him?
Yeah, I got along with -- all right with all of them.
Isn't he a little hard to get along with?
Not really, no.
No.
His big problem is drinking, too, see.
Yeah.
And when he gets drunk, he doesn't care about anybody.
No.
Anybody, as far as that's concerned.
He's a different type of guy from Bob Haggert, really.
Oh, well, Bob doesn't drink.
No.
Bob used to drink.
Yeah.
And that's the reason why he went on the wagon. He's an A.A., Bob Haggert.
Oh, is he?
Sure.
Is he?
And so he and his wife both went on that together, see. So he doesn't drink anything.
Oh, I see. But Yank --
Offer him a drink. He doesn't know how to say no. But he's a nice guy. He's like Mr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. He gets drunk and that's -- his big problem is his drinking. But he's a great guy.
Oh, I'm so glad to hear you say that.
Yeah, he really is.
And, of course, -- so Ed Hall was with the band.

Oh, I see. That one thing.
So, --

Yeah.
So --
But they're welcome, they're always
welcome.

Yeah.

Which when I was with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, I missed about three of the parties.

With the Jazz Band, and they wouldn't make it.
Yeah.
They were angry with Dick about something, you know, and that's the way it was.

And then when I left the band, I left because I'd moved out here. Well, they wouldn't send for me to do a gig in New York, staying or the state or something like that.
Yeah.
They wouldn't do that.

And Dick would. He would -- because I was the drummer in the band, see. Instead, they got Bobby ten Rosengard and -- to make the short gigs, and when they'd come

That's it.

And the kids. At the time they liked it. My wife really liked it.

Oh, I see. She just liked how it was out here.

So, she liked it.

You were one of the first people who wanted to move out of New York. Since then a lot of people have, but at the time people weren't moving out so fast, were they?

No.

Que paso?

See, like, MacShann, he -- they had a date for MacShann.

Last year.

Which was very nice.

That's nice. How about that?
Yeah. And --
They have a good band?
Yeah, we played it -- we was playing at the College Inn then.

Beautiful.

That was my first set of drums that was
just given to me.

You know, just given to me.
How nice. Isn't that wonderful? Yeah.

But Buddy came there and just tore him up. And he
-- and Jesse Price said, 'You know, he can play drums, can't he?' I said, I told you, he just whupped you all over the place.
How funny.
(Laughter.)
Well, listen, you said too Louis Bellson is one of the guys you admired.
Oh, yes, he's terrific. He plays so clean, till it sounds to me like he's reading it out of the book, he just plays so clean.
And yet, he can swing.

He sounded very good in Ellington's band.

Big, heavy band and he could move that band, couldn't he?
He certainly did. He moved that band, too.
Yeah, yeah. That's nice. Yeah.

Is he? I don't know him real well. He's a very sweet guy.

He's a very nice guy.
Fine guy. And Norman Granz used to give -- have dinners for the guys, you know.

And we went down to this Chinese place, and Norman bought all the food.
Wasn't that nice?
And we had a big eating contest.
Oh, for heaven's sake.
And that includes everybody that was on the concert.
Isn't that wonderful?
And guess who won the contest in eating?
I don't know.
Louis Belson was still eating after everybody was finished.
Isn't that unbelievable? What an amazing thing.
And Pearl Bailey was still eating.
Isn't that funny?
We couldn't eat any more. Eddie Jones, the bass player?
Yeah.
He couldn't eat no more. I was full,
Oscar Petersen, he couldn't eat any more. There was Louis Bellson, still eating.
That's funny, isn't it?
Basie couldn't eat any more.
That's funny.
I'm telling you, it was just one of those things, like we used to have drinking contests between Oscar Petersen and Norman Granz. They were going to drink each other under the table.

Hawkins.

Buck?

This Mumbles." Well, he used to do that, just sitting in the band with Basie before he ever --

-- made that record.
